title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] recently been studying prompt engineering through a human-centered (developer-centered) lens. here are some fun tips i’ve learned that don’t involve acronyms or complex words
────────
[2/9] if you don’t exactly specify the structure you want the response to take on, down to the headers or parentheses or valid attributes, the response structure may vary between LLM calls / it is not amenable to production
────────
[3/9] don’t underestimate the power of eyeballing responses—there’s no faster way to improve prompts, no matter how unprincipled it feels. IMO most early versions of prompts fail bc they’re ambiguous, and we know from DB & HCI lit that refining query ambiguity without dev input is hard
────────
[4/9] play around with the simplest prompt you can think of & run it a bunch of times on different inputs to build intuition for how LLMs “behave” for your task. then start adding instructions to your prompt in the form of rules, e.g., “do not do X”
────────
[5/9] there’s a lot to gain from good UX engineering. eg if you know the LLM does badly on a certain class of input queries, reject those queries, use default rules, or communicate uncertainty. train your end users to be as good at consuming/eyeballing LLM outputs as you are
────────
[6/9] for Q&A chatbots where prompts involve some sources for the LLM to generate an answer from, LLMs don’t always “behave” similarly for each topic of input questions. Some topics are more prone to hallucination than others. do the work to understand the failure topics/modes
────────
[7/9] for production cases where a human isn’t checking every LLM response before it’s served to an user, enforce a min & max length (eg num words or characters) for the response. even the best LLMs occasionally violate them but you can usually rerun the LLM & it’ll work
────────
[8/9] gotta go to work but will post more as I get time. I’ve been kinda quiet on this app (this year has been particularly challenging, work-wise) but I’m hoping to contribute more to the discourse
────────
[9/9] UX eng part 2: for example, if you know LLM responses are mid when the response doesn’t repeat some keywords from the prompt, highlight the keywords when displaying a response, so end users implicitly expect that. then when responses don’t have highlights, it’s an anomaly

summary:
[1/5] A big problem in monitoring LLM chains is knowing what to monitor. Most people wait until v2 or v3 of their chain to invest in eval & monitoring efforts! We’re building SPADE ♠️, a tool to give you custom evals to run in prod from day 0, ✨ just based on your prompts ✨
Quoting @LangChain
Sick of debugging finicky LLM apps? 😫
Introducing ♠️ SPADE, a tool that automatically generates tests from prompt refinements! 🧪
Paste any prompt from the LangChain Hub and it will tailor eval recommendations using prompt deltas. 🔁
SPADE analyzes version history to suggest custom Python tests. Checks format, content constraints, and more! 📏
Don't have prompts in the Hub yet? No worries! Uploading a full prompt string works as well. 📝
Try the latest research from @sh_reya at UC Berkeley to make LLM dev way more robust!
🔗
🙋‍♂️ Interested? Fill out the form to connect with the research team.
🔗
Hub:
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/tweet_video_thumb/F-bQYd4bcAABiMF.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/tweet_video/F-bQYd4bcAABiMF.mp4
────────
[2/5] I’m really excited about ♠️ because most people don’t understand that writing good evals for your chains can be just as hard as prompt engineering to build the chain. Somehow you need to distill free form output into metrics you can aggregate (ie numbers) & that imply “good”
────────
[3/5] You need to understand LLM-specific failure modes for your tasks, what end users care about, what is high-stakes, what is low-stakes, and more. If this knowledge isn’t codified into eval functions, it’s lost in tribal knowledge
────────
[4/5] Most people are evaluating LLM responses based on vibe checks. Makes sense, because vibe checks are really the best way to assess response quality right now. The ♠️ vision is to help every prompt engineer/LLM chain developer turn vibe checks into a set of interpretable evals 🪄
────────
[5/5] Wrote a blog post if you wanna learn about how it works

summary:
[1/4] i think in MLOps we were better at evaluating whether to retrain on new data vs write post-model guardrails for bad outputs. with LLMs we're prompt engineering the last mile, e.g., "do NOT say X otherwise you WILL GET FIRED" instead of checking for a substring & reprompting
────────
[2/4] some theories:
1. new data collection + model retraining is a headache (esp. for key models in production), so if a guardrail suffices, that might be more desirable
────────
[3/4] 2. prompt engineering is globally exhausting but locally desirable. a prompt may go from "don't say X" -> "do NOT say X" -> "do NOT say X otherwise you'll get fired" -> "do NOT say X otherwise you WILL GET FIRED". the diff is easier to write than the assertion & reprompting logic
────────
[4/4] 3. people without SWE or ML or even coding backgrounds turn to LLMs because they are more accessible. their actions may be limited to prompt engineering

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] We all know LLMs make mistakes. One simply cannot deploy LLM pipelines without assertions, yet writing good assertions is tedious & hard. So, we built SPADE, a system that analyzes prompts & auto-generates custom assertions in low-data settings:
────────
[2/7] I have 2 favorite contributions. First, we use prompt version history to seed candidate assertions. From studying prompt datasets, we discovered a novel insight: people implicitly encode failure criteria in revisions of their prompts, e.g., “do not say X.”
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GD-q3OSboAAR6p_.jpg
────────
[3/7] With small datasets (~50-80) of LLM pipeline inputs & outputs, we demonstrate solutions that work for 9 LLM pipelines across various domains (e.g., finance, software, writing). The data and pipelines are open-sourced for further research on deployed LLMs.
────────
[4/7] Second, we filter bad & redundant candidate assertions without sampling lots of data or training custom evaluators. We formulate this as a problem of selecting a minimal set of non-overlapping and accurate assertions while maintaining coverage.
────────
[5/7] We analyzed 19 LLM pipelines from @langchain, creating a taxonomy of prompt changes to develop assertions around. For example, if a developer adds an “exclusion instruction,” we synthesize assertion(s) to check for this.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GD-q_iraAAAwWy6.jpg
────────
[6/7] Currently, we’re exploring how to put SPADE in an interactive system for anyone to use. Thanks to Haotian Li, @pgasawa, @MadelonHulsebos, Yiming Lin, @jdzamfi, @hwchase17, @WHinthorn, @adityagp, and @sirrice for a fun collaboration---looking forward to our future work! 🥳
────────
[7/7] Personally, I’m grateful to work on a project with fun research problems and practical potential. Our community has only scratched the surface of what LLMs can do & what to deploy. I’m excited by the work we’re all doing to make them more reliable for automated use.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] did a small audit of my historical chat gpt queries & was so surprised to find that almost all of them were related to my job. at first glance, my clusters of tasks seemed similar, but i thought some more and realized they require different “reasoning” abilities
────────
[2/10] - writing conciseness tasks: “rewrite {x} to be more concise but maintain my simplicity, clarity, and all the content”
- outline-to-doc writing tasks: “generate a short postmortem document from the following content”
────────
[3/10] - latex wrangling tasks: “create a latex table from this data {markdown or google sheets snippet} using booktabs” or “create a tikz figure of {image or text description of the layout}”
- latex “formalization” tasks: “choose a Greek symbol” or “make this {definition} more formal”
────────
[4/10] - coding algorithms tasks: “write a function that randomly shuffles a collection of documents proportional to some weights”
- tool-specific coding tasks: “implement the functions in the class below to load and save from GCS” or “add a section in my streamlit app to do {X}”
────────
[5/10] been thinking about why I don’t use LLMs for non work related activities (eg cooking, training my dog, traveling). my go-to for other hobbies is TikTok. I like that on TikTok I can passively learn/watch content by scrolling
────────
[6/10] - data wrangling tasks: “convert this sequence {list of numbered elems} to a Python list” or “list rows from this {table} that are related to {x}”
- frontend component styling tasks
- create images for slides (i actually wrote a custom gpt to do this to maintain style)
────────
[7/10] I also develop taste by understanding what other humans do (not necessarily what LLMs say in chat), and for my hobbies I’m more interested in taste than being productive. Eg I’d rather look at what Nara Smith cooks than actually do what she does, so she & I need different tools
────────
[8/10] I guess I’m also hesitant to use LLMs for things I am not trained by human experts to do. I have no trouble using it for coding and tasks I can super easily verify. But I’m well aware of how unreliable LLMs are and I’m too nervous to use them for tasks I’m not good at myself
────────
[9/10] There’s a high cost for bad LLM responses for tasks I don’t know how to do. For example, I started learning to bake bread. It takes SO long to iterate & took me 4 TikTok recipes to bake something that wasn’t flat. If I was iterating through LLM-generated recipes I’d have given up
────────
[10/10] Another interesting observation about using TikTok to begin a hobby: when I started learning to bake bread, I didn’t even know what I was supposed to learn. I didn’t know what hydration, shaping, etc mean. Sure an LLM can describe this in a response to “how do I bake bread” but

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] i'm surprised by LLMs' unreliability in reasonable-scale data generation tasks, like crafting 250-word product descriptions from details & reviews. hallucination actually isn't the biggest problem i'm seeing; it's poor data quality and LLMs' failure to follow prompt instructions
────────
[2/4] consider a product description generation task and some Amazon product reviews dataset. the prompt will include instructions on how to write an SEO-optimized description, desired word limit, & not to sabotage the product/say anything negative, even if the reviews are negative
────────
[3/4] i did this for ~150 products with gpt-3.5-turbo, and here's the common errors i saw:
1) not between 0.5 * word_limit and 1.5 * word_limit words
2) sabotaging the product by rephrasing a bad review (e.g., "these may not be the greatest, but they provide good value for money")
────────
[4/4] 3) data quality. typos in the reviews get spit out verbatim in the generated description
4) data quality. when preprocessing text, unicode characters change (e.g., trademark symbol becomes tm and is appended to a word)
5) data quality. the review is not for the product

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] Evals are arguably the hardest part of LLMOps. LLMs mess up, so we check them w/ other LLMs, but this feels icky. Who validates the validators??
We built an interface to align LLM-based evals with user preferences, learning a lot about why this is hard:
────────
[2/7] We created a system to help generate & validate eval functions based on user-defined good and bad LLM outputs. We did a study with expert LLM practitioners & found that the challenge in writing evals isn't the effort—which users are willing to invest—but due to "criteria drift."
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GLxxmqaaEAAvBUS.png
────────
[3/7] As people observe patterns in LLM behavior, especially if the pattern conflicts with some implicit criteria they had in mind, they rethink whether this criteria should exist, or how the criteria should be adapted to reflect what the LLM is good or bad at doing.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GLxyELIa0AAshfy.png
────────
[4/7] As people observe more LLM outputs and grade them, their criteria "drifts", or gets refined. This doesn't entirely stop; and some criteria are dependent on the specific LLM outputs observed (and hence prompt and model).
────────
[5/7] We are improving our system before we release it (hopefully in the near future). I am grateful for my fantastic co-authors (@jdzamfi, @bjo3rn, @adityagp, @IanArawjo) and the LLM practitioners who generously gave us their time. For more insights, please read the preprint!
────────
[6/7] People cannot write LLM evals they trust without looking at LLM outputs. People cannot improve prompts without evals they trust. While automated systems can *assist* people in co-evolving prompts and evals, humans need to be in the loop to validate the validators.
────────
[7/7] Criteria drift raises serious questions for tools that assume the independence of evaluation from regular human observation of model outputs. The vision that prompt (or LLM application) engineering can be *entirely* automated is misguided!

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] Can’t overstate the importance of this. For a while I felt that the vibes were off in the tools that try to automate all of LLM pipeline dev (eg RAG hyperparams), but I couldn’t explain why. For LLMs, evals aren’t a fixed set of criteria & good and bad outputs
Quoting @sh_reya
Criteria drift raises serious questions for tools that assume the independence of evaluation from regular human observation of model outputs. The vision that prompt (or LLM application) engineering can be *entirely* automated is misguided!
────────
[2/4] If you’re trying to bring “auto-ML” to LLM pipeline development and you try various configurations of prompts/hyperparameters, humans kinda need to be in the loop to evaluate those pipeline configs’ LLM outputs, bc their eval criteria drifts (eg kinda depends on outputs).
────────
[3/4] Of course there are probably some applications with less drift, like applications where there is only one right answer—and thus “accuracy” is a more meaningful metric—but many generative AI applications use LLMs for tasks that could, in theory, have millions of good outputs.
────────
[4/4] @stogachess Considering how nondeterministic these end to end LLM pipelines can be (eg prompts change, LLMs change, vector db indexes change), I think the problem is important and hard to study!

Today, we're introducing 🔄 Self-Improving LLM Judges in @Autoblocks.
​
LLM judges are an amazing way to evaluate subjective LLM app outputs at scale. The problem is — they're usually too inaccurate for teams to rely on.
​
This forces teams to lean entirely on experts to review LLM app outputs, which is both slow and expensive.
​
Self-Improving LLM Judges fix this and are basically a way to automatically improve LLM judge accuracy using expert preferences. They don't replace expert reviews but augment them.
​
One of our early adopters, a Series C healthcare startup using LLMs, reported a 75%+ improvement (!) in the accuracy of a critical LLM judge after just one month of using Self-Improving LLM Judges.

[2/8] when we wrote the Who Validates the Validators paper a few months later, it seemed like people trusted LLMs-as-a-judge more if they were fully aware of the alignment process, but still, people would never ship it

[5/8] embracing LLM-as-a-judge for quick prototyping, committing to evolving metric sets, datasets, LLM applications, doing the work to label their data, etc

[6/8] and it is really cool to see people rip out their infra stack, blindly rely on vendors a little less, and build their systems more from first principles with an eye towards bespoke metrics,

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Love this summary of & key insight from my recent blog post on data flywheels for LLM applications. It’s interesting to see what resonates, particularly continuous human involvement, and new ideas people haven’t thought about, like agents for adapting eval metric definitions
Quoting @_philschmid
How can we dynamically improve LLM applications using production data? @sh_reya outlines ideas for building a continuous Data Flywheel. 👀
1. Evaluation: Define success metrics that align with specific use cases. Implement both simple code functions and LLM-as-a-judge techniques to evaluate outputs.
2. Monitoring: Automate metric re-evaluation and keep implementations aligned with criteria using recent and human-aligned examples.
3. Continual Improvement: Iterate on prompts and pipelines based on metric performance.
Insights:
👨‍💼 - Humans need to be in the loop for evaluation.
🤖 - Use LLM-as-a-judge for subjective metric evaluation.
📊 - Regularly sample and (re-)label production data to align with evolving goals.
🔍 - Few-shot examples can improve production and evaluation performance.
💡 - Use an LLM agent to propose new metrics and update existing ones.
✅ - Validate inputs as well, e.g. language, complexity, PII.
1️⃣ - Binary Metrics are easier to align with human experts.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GSggjiYWEAAPEhI.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] the biggest barrier to fine tuning LLMs is not cost or modeling or systems expertise anymore, but in collecting high-quality data. it’s hard to do for custom tasks. people try to use gpt 4 as a data generator, which seems ok at a glance but is full of random mistakes at scale
────────
[2/5] my research interests are now expanding to democratizing fine tuning (esp for people who aren’t ML experts or have high data literacy)…interestingly even if you implement good filtering for gpt 4 generated data (or synthetic data) fine tuned models still make lots of mistakes
────────
[3/5] so it becomes important to also repair the bad synthetic data, and possibly even augment the synthetic data to increase representation for common failure modes
────────
[4/5] obviously repairing custom data for custom tasks requires domain expertise (which domain experts are happy to provide), but I am very curious if it is possible to scale up human-guided data repair for LLMs
────────
[5/5] augmentation is very difficult for people who are not very data literate. it’s hard to know that you need to generate more data in areas that LLMs are bad at & how to do it. thinking about ways to automate both data repair & augmentation for custom tasks/pipelines…stay tuned

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (15 tweets)
summary:
[1/15] LLM pipeline programming is too imperative. declarative LLM frameworks (i.e., that let users specify LLM tasks at a “high level” and turn this spec or query into executable code) are so difficult to get right
────────
[2/15] first, it is not clear what the logical building blocks are. LLM capabilities change daily. should “chain of thought” or “react” really be logical building blocks? should “RAG” even be a building block? imo these are “physical” operations, to use DB speak
────────
[3/15] so maybe, in an ideal framework, you have a “map” (or “select”/projection, to use DB terminology) type operator that transforms an input into some output with a prompt, and the details of how this is executed is left to the system (eg CoT, retries, repeating/self-refinement)
────────
[4/15] in an ideal framework, each building block serves a different logical purpose, and users should not have to experiment with different building blocks (this should be the job of the engine compiling/optimizing/building the executable)
────────
[5/15] my second big point is, since LLMs have varying accuracy, frameworks have to do experimentation. say I want to convert a table w/ 100k rows to a common schema. doing this all in one prompt may miss a bunch of rows. maybe I’ll have better luck converting 1k or 10k rows at a time
────────
[6/15] from a framework designer perspective, there are no semantics for what LLMs can and can’t do. Anything one says in the prompt could work?? yucky. performance is model-specific and task-specific and data-specific
────────
[7/15] types are tricky. suppose the input is a string, a comma-separated list of objects (with typos), & the prompt says to find the most common object. should the op type be a reduce/aggregation, bc that’s what the prompt says? or a map, since one string/csv gets mapped to one output?
────────
[8/15] more excitingly we are moving to an era where the gains from random prompting tricks like “think step by step” are minuscule compared to, simply, writing clearer instructions
────────
[9/15] in a true declarative framework one would simply have to write something like “ common_schema)”, and the result will be a new table for each original table, and this just works, no matter the size of the tables or the data
────────
[10/15] something that has emerged is: the interface we design has to be iterative (people don’t know what they want a good result to look like until they see it). eg, to find common themes and supporting quotes across product reviews, one has to see how many themes arise in the first
────────
[11/15] we’ve mostly been focused on thinking about the systems part & optimizing for accuracy. given a high-level MapReduce-like task, what’s the most accurate execution plan? see my website to learn more about our DocETL project, still working on docs, cleaning up the paper draft, etc
────────
[12/15] I & colleagues are thinking a lot these days about how we can design interfaces and frameworks that focus on eliciting clearer instructions from humans & offloading the selection of the most accurate plan or pipeline to a system
────────
[13/15] looking forward to sharing more in the next couple of weeks!!
────────
[14/15] so this begs the question, what is the job of the system/optimizer/declarative framework?? to find **accurate** plans for the given task spec, ideally within **interactive latencies**
────────
[15/15] pass, determine if they want more or less, or finer or coarser granularity, then change the prompt to give the number of themes. **task specification is not known upfront** and for LLMs/intelligent pipelines, may never be known upfront. people iterate on the task specifications

[2/9] 3/ But even for Gemini 1.5 Pro (2M token context limit), when given the entire dataset at once, it only reports on the evolution of 5 themes across all the debates! And, the reports get progressively worse as the output goes on.

[3/9] 2/ Let's illustrate DocETL with an example task: analyzing presidential debates over the last 40 years to see what topics candidates discussed, & how the viewpoints of Democrats and Republicans evolved. The combined debate transcripts span ~740k words, exceeding context limits of most LLMs.

────────
[5/9] 4/ How does DocETL solve this problem? Users declaratively specify a simple pipeline of operators, with a map operation to extract topics and viewpoints for each debate transcript, and a reduce operation to generate a report of viewpoints for each theme.

We have been working on DocETL for a while, actually (since the first gpt-4 API came out). We even wrote a couple of papers on LLM-powered evals, since DocETL critically relies on it. I always thought that at some point, someone will come out with a unstructured data processing benchmark, since it's a multi-billion dollar industry that no LLM solves off-the-shelf without manual task decomposition. But no one has done it yet!!
The more we work on DocETL and apply it to various tasks, the more I see how difficult it would be to teach LLMs to do data processing at training time or plan it in token space at inference time. LLMs need to be able to experiment with different plans to process data and compare them...basically LLMs need access to themselves as tools :D

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Yep, the pitfall of most declarative LLM frameworks is that they assume user-defined operations (and optimized prompts) will yield sufficiently accurate results when executed by LLMs. This is bad for data processing tasks. If an LLM can't extract all 50 clauses or statements of interest from your 100-page legal document in one call, you have to chunk up your document, run different LLM calls for different clauses, etc. Or, if your LLM can't give you a comprehensive note summary for your 300-page textbook, you have to iteratively refine the summary and manually validate the intermediate summary after every LLM call.
The reality is that people spend enormous amounts of time crafting the perfect data/task decomposition and running validations at each step. This should be the job of an optimizer. DocETL's optimizer uses LLM agents to generate candidate plans and compare sample outputs to see which plan is best.
Quoting @prashanth_pappu
Many LLM frameworks are focusing on declarative composition. That’s the easy part. The hard part is the fine tuning of LLMs at various parts of the graph which is hard to do without verifiers and HITL.
────────
[2/2] We have some exciting UX challenges & innovations ahead for HITL optimization
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GYQrc3oakAELWSx.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Great question. A streaming API is on the roadmap, but all of our LLM-powered operators are very easy to incrementally maintain. Map operations (e.g., extract topics from documents) are stateless. The stateful operations are resolve (deduplicates topics) and reduce (summarizes content/documents for each topic).
For resolve ( we maintain clusters of duplicates. On a new topic, we can use the comparison prompt to compare the new topic to an exemplar from each cluster (this can be more efficient with our blocking optimizations, also described in the docs). If there's a match, we use the resolution prompt to re-compute the canonical topic name for that cluster. In a streaming system, we just have to persist the clusters.
For reduce ( we implement a batched folding pattern, where we iteratively update some state with new documents. In a streaming system, we just have to persist the intermediate states.
Quoting @jxnlco
@sh_reya how do you handle new documents / emergent topics

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] Last week, I posted about DocETL--an open-source system we are building at Berkeley for creating and executing LLM-powered data processing pipelines.
Today, I'll talk about our resolve operator, which addresses duplicate content. 🐵🐵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GYvNhseacAADVU5.jpg
────────
[2/13] 3/ Consider analyzing customer reviews for a product. We might use an LLM to extract themes from each review. However, the LLM might express the same theme in slightly different ways!
────────
[3/13] 2/ LLMs often produce inconsistent results, even when referring to the same entity or concept. This variability can complicate downstream tasks that rely on grouping or aggregating LLM-generated data.
────────
[4/13] 7/ Blocking filters out obvious non-matches, reducing the number of necessary comparisons. DocETL leverages AI agents to synthesize task-specific blocking rules, which can be embedding-based or code-based.
────────
[5/13] 6/ The resolve operator in DocETL addresses this efficiency challenge by drawing on traditional data management techniques. It uses a two-step process: blocking and pairwise comparison.
────────
[6/13] 5/ How should we identify duplicates? The simplest interface would enable us to write an LLM prompt to compare 2 themes and apply it to all pairs. However, this approach scales poorly, requiring O(n^2) LLM calls--which is prohibitively expensive for even small datasets.
────────
[7/13] 4/ For instance, "battery life" could be expressed as "long-lasting battery" or "excellent battery performance." These variations, while semantically similar, are textually distinct. To effectively summarize reviews by theme, we need to deduplicate and canonicalize them.
────────
[8/13] 10/ Complementing this, DocETL also generates code-based blocking rules. These are Python statements designed to quickly filter out obvious non-matches. They might include checks for exact matches on certain fields, length comparisons, or other logical conditions. Here are some examples for checking patient names:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GYvRF8XbQAEQ40u.jpg
────────
[9/13] 9/ DocETL then determines a cosine similarity threshold that achieves a target recall of true matches (e.g., 95%) based on the LLM-powered comparison results. Then, during execution, pairs with similarity < threshold are filtered out, significantly reducing LLM calls.
────────
[10/13] 8/ Embedding-based blocking relies on a similarity threshold to determine potential matches To come up with this threshold, the optimizer:
1. Samples 100s of pairs & runs the comparison prompt on them
2. Calculates similarities for the pairs (in embedding space)
────────
[11/13] 12/ Anyways, this dual approach to blocking allows DocETL to handle a wide variety of entity resolution scenarios, adapting to the specific characteristics of each dataset and resolution task. Excitingly, by synthesizing these rules automatically with LLM agents, DocETL lessens the burden of manual rule creation, making entity resolution much more accessible ☺️
────────
[12/13] 11/ These code-based rules work in disjunction with the embedding-based rules. This means that pairs must pass at least one rule (not all rules) to proceed to the LLM comparison stage. This is super powerful--we can specify selective code-based blocking rules if the embedding-based still has high recall, so the code-based rules can capture potential matches that embedding similarity may not!
────────
[13/13] 13/13 Learn more about the resolve operator here:
And stay tuned for more deep dives (and our upcoming paper) ✨

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] DocETL is our agentic system for LLM-powered data processing pipelines. Time for this week’s technical deep dive on _gleaning_, our automated technique to improve accuracy by iteratively refining outputs 🧠🔍 (using LLM-as-judge!)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GZTnGW_bwAATsvP.png
────────
[2/8] 2/ LLMs often don't return perfect results on the first try. Consider extracting insights from user logs with an LLM. An LLM might miss important behaviors or include extraneous information. These issues could lead to misguided product decisions or wasted engineering efforts.
────────
[3/8] 5/ Here's how gleaning works: there are two LLMs: a generator and a validator LLM. The generator comes up with the initial output. The validator assess it to see if refinement is needed. If so, it provides refinement feedback to the generator LLM (e.g., "there's a better example of X pattern earlier in the document to include in the output"). The two LLMs go back & forth until the validator LLM has no more feedback for the generator (or max rounds reached).
────────
[4/8] 4/ We were inspired by the GraphRAG paper ( which introduces gleaning as a way to repeatedly extract more entities from an LLM when building a knowledge graph over a collection of documents. We generalize it to any task/any data, not just entity extraction!
────────
[5/8] 3/ DocETL's gleaning feature uses the power of LLMs themselves to validate and refine their own outputs, creating a self-improving loop that significantly boosts output quality.
────────
[6/8] 8/ Implementing gleaning in DocETL is straightforward. You specify a validation_prompt and num_rounds in your pipeline configuration. DocETL handles the rest, managing the iterative refinement process behind the scenes.
────────
[7/8] 7/ For our user log analysis example, a validation prompt might ask:
a) Is the report well-structured for someone to easily determine how to improve the productL
b) Is there important info in the logs missing from the report?
c) Is everything in the report important & originating from the source (i.e., no hallucinations)?
────────
[8/8] 11/ Learn more about gleaning & validation in our docs: and stay tuned for more interesting technical deep dives! There are many ways to join in on the fun—star the repo, or join our Discord server :-)

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] DocETL continues to evolve as a powerful system for LLM-powered data processing & analysis pipelines. Since I'm at UIST this week, this deep dive focuses on UI/UX insights for transforming unstructured data with LLMs--on complex tasks and the art of prompt engineering 🧠🔧
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GZ8lvI6XgAEhtEU.jpg
────────
[2/9] 4/ Consider the concept of a "theme." Maybe users can't precisely define it (in part, that's why they're asking the LLM to identify them); but, users can provide valuable feedback on theme extraction after seeing initial results. This necessitates an iterative approach where users can indirectly give feedback.
────────
[3/9] 3/ Why is such a task multi-operation? A common pattern we are seeing is map-resolve-reduce pipelines: map each document to 1+ themes & insights, resolve/canonicalize themes, and then reduce/summarize each insight set for each theme
────────
[4/9] 2/ Complex tasks in unstructured data analysis are inherently pipelines of multiple operations. Users may need to construct these operations incrementally. Fuzzy multi-operation analysis tasks like "generate summaries for themes in documents"
────────
[5/9] 6/ And analysts themselves may not know how to define this until they have built some intuition for how companies discuss these themes/concepts in the report. As such, there is no world where analysts will not iterate on their prompt/operation!!
────────
[6/9] 5/ Let's use a concrete example: analyzing climate-related reports from companies to find common patterns in carbon neutrality plans. This task asks LLMs to identify relevant snippets from hundreds of pages of documents. "relevant" or "plan to go reduce co2 emissions" must be defined in the prompt
────────
[7/9] 9/ UI is still a work in progress, but as always, we invite you to star our repo, join our Discord server (there are 230 people already!), and stay tuned for more technical deep dives into DocETL! 🚀📊
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/ext_tw_video_thumb/1846234729277706240/pu/img/rda9pM4Y-NAwsPSh.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/ext_tw_video/1846234729277706240/pu/vid/avc1/470x270/hg8M-oVLBqASIwXH.mp4?tag=12
────────
[8/9] 8/ As we are building our UI, to facilitate iteration and help users program LLMs for unstructured data analysis, we're exploring several techniques:
* Running operations on data samples (for interactive latencies)
* Enabling users to "save" or annotate outputs for use in subsequent system prompts
* Visualizations (e.g., distributions of themes, counts per reduce group when reducing on an LLM-generated key)
* Implementing dynamically-synthesized, task-specific "pushes" to refine output (e.g., "make it shorter", "use bullet points")
────────
[9/9] 7/ More generally, users might want themes to be more fine-grained or broader, shorter or longer, more or less relevant to specific topics. The key insight is that people cannot effectively write AI-powered data operations without seeing and refining the output.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (12 tweets)
summary:
[1/12] Our (first) DocETL preprint is now on Arxiv! "DocETL: Agentic Query Rewriting and Evaluation for Complex Document Processing" It has been almost 2 years in the making, so I am very happy we hit this milestone :-)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gabg3A5WAAAhsyw.jpg
────────
[2/12] DocETL is a framework for LLM-powered unstructured data processing and analysis. The big new idea in this paper is to automatically rewrite user-specified pipelines into a sequence of finer-grained and more accurate operators.
────────
[3/12] Rewriting an LLM-powered operation on a long or complex document isn't as simple as chunking up the document and applying the operation to each chunk, then unifying the results. Often a chunk cannot be processed by itself (there's "peripheral" context in other chunks that will clarify the chunk content). The gather operator "gathers" such peripheral context.
────────
[4/12] I'll mention two big contributions in this paper. First, we present a rich suite of operators, with three entirely new operators to deal with decomposing complex documents: the split, gather, and resolve operators.
────────
[5/12] Second, we introduce 13 pipeline-level rewrite directives that yield logically-equivalent pipelines. We built an agentic query optimizer that uses LLMs to implement these rewrite directives, if they apply to the user-written pipeline.
────────
[6/12] The resolve operator helps when applying LLM operations to individual units of data & grouping by results and aggregating them. It resolves inconsistencies in LLM outputs.
────────
[7/12] There are many more neat ideas in the preprint, as well as some case studies. Please read it to learn more. I was very surprised by how well DocETL's optimizer worked out of the box. I am optimistic that this will only improve as LLMs get better.
────────
[8/12] In our optimizer, we also evaluate all the candidate plans that arise from rewrites. We execute plans on data samples and use LLMs to compare outputs. This draws on our line of work on LLM-powered evaluation over the last year (SPADE in VLDB 2024, EvalGen in UIST 2024, PromptEvals in ARR 2024).
────────
[9/12] What's interesting here is that there can be many instantiations of a rewrite directive. For example, one can break a map operation down into a chain of map calls in many different ways. Rewrite directives are heavily inspired by the Cascades framework for query optimization, but designed for the new age of LLMs. Interestingly, LLMs are quite good at coming up with new operation prompts given the original prompts and samples of data.
────────
[10/12] This project would not be possible without great people and resources: thank you to the CLEAN team for onboarding me to the police misconduct task and workflows (and inspiring a couple of rewrite directives), my labmates for helping brainstorm with me whenever I felt stuck, and profs Aditya (@adityagp) and Eugene (@sirrice) for mentorship. Also, thank you to Aditya for coordinating LLM resources; this project blew through many thousands of dollars of credits 🤣
────────
[11/12] We have a bunch of other projects in our pipeline, all around human-centered, interactive, and AI-powered unstructured data processing. There are some neat data & AI contributions underway (eg fast and accurate infinite-context reduce) as well as HCI contributions (eg human-AI collaborative optimization). Very excited for these next several months.
────────
[12/12] Finally, DocETL is open source! We also have a discord server. Check out our post from a few weeks ago introducing it:
Please try it out and let us know what you think!
Quoting @sh_reya
LLMs have made exciting progress on hard tasks! But they still struggle to analyze complex, unstructured documents (including today's Gemini 1.5 Pro 002).
We (UC Berkeley) built 📜DocETL, an open-source, low-code system for LLM-powered data processing:
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GYQTflwakAIhEOS.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] I have a lot of thoughts on this as someone who has manually combed through hundreds of humans' prompt deltas
Quoting @simonw
I know they're popular - and offered by both OpenAI and Anthropic, who should really know if they work - but I can't help being skeptical of tools that help write prompts for you
I just don't see why an LLM would be good at prompting an LLM
────────
[2/9] there's a lot of literature on LLM sensemaking from the HCI community here (our own "who validates the validators" paper is one of many), but I still think LLM sensemaking is woefully unexplored, especially with respect to the stage in the mlops lifecycle
────────
[3/9] first, humans tend to underspecify the first version of their prompt. if they're in the right environment where they can get a near-instantaneous LLM response in the same interface (e.g., chatgpt, Claude, openai playground), they just want to see what the llm can do
────────
[4/9] for example (see our docetl paper), if you are an investigative journalist and want an LLM to find all instances of police misconduct in a report/document, you have to define misconduct. there are many types of misconduct, each of which also may require their own definitions
────────
[5/9] second, humans derive a lot of the prompt content based on their sensemaking. if they observe a weird output, they edit their prompt (usually by adding another instruction). many of these edits are clarifications/definitions
────────
[6/9] not only do people want to just see what the LLM can do, but they also don't fully know what they are supposed to say in the prompt, or what answer they want (they won't know it until they see it).
I think of a prompt as a form you need to fill out to submit your task to the LLM, and the fields of this form are unknown and dynamic (i.e., task-specific). a prompt writing tool can make these fields more known
────────
[7/9] overall I think prompting is going to be a collaborative effort between humans and LLMs in the future. humans alone are limited; LLM-written prompts alone are limited (you need to have _some_ human input and feedback to solve the human's fuzzy or underspecified task).
────────
[8/9] third, with docetl (our AI-powered data processing tool), some of our users don't have lots of programming experience, and as a result, I've sent them starter pipelines they can use to process their data.
surprisingly many of them can move forward without me, tweaking pipeline prompts, editing them, adding new operations, etc. I think an AI assistant can do my job of initially drafting the pipeline
────────
[9/9] the LLM-generated prompt writer is GREAT here to relieve blank page syndrome for defining important terms in prompts. if I ask Claude to generate a prompt for "find all instances of police misconduct in this document", it makes an attempt to start definitions, which I can then refine
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GbLzarPakAIa5BP.png

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Whenever I talk to ML/AI researchers, many are surprised that complex and long document processing with LLMs is so hard. I find it strange how little attention (comparatively) is given to this, given that data processing probably has the highest market cap of all applications
Quoting @tgatte
@antgoldbloom @DynamicWebPaige It’s not being ignored. @marqueeinsights has been doing this work with large and mid-size enterprises for over 4 years. GenAI makes it easier to do non-labeled extraction but it struggles with large documents. It’s not perfect but usually better than human copy/paste.
────────
[2/3] Second, there seems to be an unawareness of queries people have over unstructured data. This is probably because many people make up example queries and try to shove them to customers, like pointwise lookups in documents. This is not the only query type. People have complex questions in the vein of “help me make sense of this data” which is not a set of specific NL questions that can be answered via a RAG system
────────
[3/3] First, I think there is a broad unawareness of the benefits of a declarative query interface. Every genAI x data startup sells one LLM pipeline or feature (eg turn document into podcast) where engineers have manually tuned every LLM step or call in their pipeline. This is bespoke, costly in resources, and doesn’t scale. A **very** nice problem is how to give such querying a declarative interface

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] what makes LLM frameworks feel unusable is that there's still so much burden for the user to figure out the bespoke amalgamation of LLM calls to ensure end-to-end accuracy. in we've found that relying on an agent to do this requires lots of scaffolding
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gbj57Eoa0AAZ0xw.jpg
────────
[2/5] to solve this problem, DocETL uses hand-defined rewrite directives that can enumerate theoretically-equivalent decompositions/pipeline rewrites. the agent is then limited to creating prompts/output schemas for newly synthesized operations, according to the rewrite rules, which bounds its errors.
────────
[3/5] first there needs to be a way of getting theoretically valid task decompositions. simply asking an LLM to break down a complex task over lots of data may result in a logically incorrect plan. for example, the LLM might choose the wrong data operation (projection instead of aggregation), and this would be a different pipeline entirely.
────────

Quoting @jxnlco
Why Startups Struggle to Hire AI Engineers
The question keeps coming up: Why can't startups hire talented AI engineers? The answer isn't complicated, but it might be hard to swallow. Top AI talent today has unprecedented leverage. When I was working full-time, my W2 showed $580,000 in salary. Now, consulting independently, I'm looking at $800,000-900,000 in revenue. Against this backdrop, a startup offering $170,000 and equity that might be worth nothing isn't just unappealing—it's a non-starter.
But compensation isn't the whole story. In my experience working with companies to hire AI talent, I've noticed that the best engineers consistently ask two penetrating questions: Is this product actually defensible? And do the founders truly understand AI's capabilities and limitations? They're really asking: "Am I going to be hired to perform magic?"
This is where I've found I can add the most value to startups—by helping them craft a strategic roadmap that serves three crucial purposes. First, it provides actual tactics and strategy: how to collect data, conduct evaluations, and systematically improve the product. Second, it becomes a powerful tool for attracting talent by demonstrating technical credibility and realistic expectations. Finally, it serves as a compelling narrative for fundraising, showing investors a clear path to value creation.
The roadmap needs to show more than just technical sophistication. It needs to demonstrate an understanding of AI's limitations and include clear guardrails for communicating capabilities to users. When I see founders who don't get this, I've sometimes returned their money rather than help them pursue an unrealistic vision.
For startups wondering why they can't hire great AI talent, the answer often lies in this gap between expectations and reality. With the current upside of AI skills being so high, top engineers can afford to be selective. They're looking for more than just a paycheck—they want evidence that founders understand the technology they're building with and have a realistic plan for success.
Without a compelling technical strategy that addresses these concerns, startups will continue to struggle in attracting the talent they need. The good news? A well-crafted roadmap can solve multiple problems at once: guiding development, attracting talent, and securing funding. But it has to be grounded in reality, not wishful thinking.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
I like this article a lot. The thesis is that AI-assisted coding tools can cause big problems for junior employees or beginners (who don’t know how to do this 30%). I agree, and I am glad we are talking about the problem, but I don’t think we realize the extent to which these tools’ UX needs to improve, irrespective of how good AI gets.
First, I want to argue that this ratio will never be 100-0. Humans struggle to perfectly communicate intent in their prompts. Only in a dystopian future would we never collaborate with the AI to refine the software it’s building; to change our intent b/c the AI helped us discover something we didn’t think about; to rephrase our prompt bc we realized it was ambiguous; etc. I would like to assume the future is not so dystopian.
Now, given the premise that AI-assisted tools should encourage collaboration, such tools must present AI-generated artifacts intuitively for humans. Nobody does this well. AIs write code differently than we do—they write file by file, rather than by concept. This is particularly stark for complex code changes. For example, if I want to add a new feature to my web app, without AI, I would break this feature down to its small components, and then implement 1 component at a time. Implementation for each component often spans multiple files (for complex features). So my implementation looks like a bunch of small edits to files (edit in file A -> edit in file B -> edit in file A again) whereas the AI will do (all edits in file A -> all edits in file B). The latter is such a pain to verify, because you have to do the work of decomposing & building a mental model for the edits—what you’d have to do without the AI!!
Current AI-assisted tools only work well for the category of tasks where the generation-(human) verification gap is quite large. Fortunately, there are many such tasks (eg basic CRUD apps, writing configs, plotting data). But they suck when the gap is small. For complex tasks, for as long as AIs solve them differently than humans do, the gap will be large. Maybe post-training will teach AIs how to present complex solutions differently. Maybe we will come up with heuristics for how much information we can present to a human at once (and how to measure this). Idk. But we have a really long way to go!
Quoting @addyosmani
"Hard truths about AI-assisted coding"
While AI-Assisted coding can get you 70% of the way there (great for prototypes or MVPs), the final 30% requires significant human intervention for quality and maintainability.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GeALLF4aIAAdxUg.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
“It means look at your logs/traces - start with 30 or so. Start categorizing the errors and issues you see. Keep looking at logs and traces until you feel like you aren't learning anything new.” 💯 this is a muscle anyone can develop—even if your SWE brain hates the uncertainty of it, I promise you will get used to it, and get really good & fast at it.
Quoting @HamelHusain
I started doing office hours on LLM evals and met with 8+ founders in the last 3 weeks. Common questions:
- Which components of our app do we start evaluating (RAG,tool calls, etc)?
- What metrics should I use?
- Where should I spend my time?
All have the same solution. LOOK AT THE DATA. What does this mean though?
It means look at your logs/traces - start with 30 or so. Start categorizing the errors and issues you see. Keep looking at logs and traces until you feel like you aren't learning anything new.
In the end, you will know where your biggest issues are. You prioritize those! You will also get a sense of what is most important to measure (and how).
That's it. Look at data, build evals and tests prioritized by patterns in the data. If you don't have data, generate synthetic inputs/interactions into your LLM application so you can generate data.
I didn't make this technique up fwiw. These are fundamentals of building machine learning systems and is often referred to as "Error Analysis". It is a fancy word for looking at data, categorizing errors, and then doing data analysis on those errors to understand what to prioritize and work on.
I've documented some of the office hours, and you can see in all cases the solution was performing error analysis. Here are links to those:

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] This is a great articulation for why we chose yaml to be the representation of DocETL pipelines. Eventually AIs will always write the first draft of pipelines. yaml is easy for AIs to write. Humans only then need to read the prompts/operations & verify that they make sense. They should not have to read Python or JS code that is not relevant to the LLM-powered data processing
Also interfaces can help accelerate verification a lot. Humans should not read code or pipelines as text. In we have affordances for viewing docetl operations (eg LLM-powered map or reduce) + sample outputs in the same screen, providing concrete feedback on outputs, and steering AIs to edit operations. Our user studies find that a seamless iterative flow really helps people get to a working LLM-generated artifact for a complex task surprisingly fast. Paper coming soon, post-holidays.
Quoting @btaylor
@rorykoehler I think this is too simplistic.
If an AI generates three million lines of code for a complex distributed system, would just reading the code be sufficient?
Likewise, I would argue most modern programming languages are designed to be written, not read for correctness. You discover most Python bugs at runtime. Perl scripts famously inscrutable to anyone but the author. What does a programming language designed to be “read” look like given we are no longer the primary authors?
I think “just read the code” is the local maximum we are at already.
────────
[2/4] Though DocETL is specific to data processing, I feel that general coding is similar in that verification is important and hard, but can be accelerated by good interfaces, speculative execution, and visualization
────────
[3/4] a snapshot of what the IDE looks like for part of a fairly complex task (finding common action plans in organizations' climate reports, with mappings to known intervention strategies). Table-level view with histograms accelerates spot-checks, to make sure the LLM's answer *roughly* aligns with your own. Expanding a column (second view) allows you to verify individual outputs and provide fine-grained feedback, which you can ask the AI assistant to aggregate & then propose prompt edits. People make extensive use of both views

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] how come nobody is talking about how much shittier eng on-calls are thanks to blind integrations of AI-generated code? LLMs are great coders but horrible engineers. no, the solution is not “prompt the LLM to write more documentation and tests” (cont.)
────────
[2/11] so the burden is on me to exhaustively test the generated app via my interactions, and then reverse engineer the mental model of what the code should be, and then eyeball the generated code to make sure this matches my model. This is so horrible to do for multi-file edits or > 800 lines of generated code (which is super common for web dev diffs)
────────
[3/11] i will take react development as an example. I use cursor but I think the problems are not specific to cursor. Every time I ask for a new feature to be added to my codebase, it almost always uses at least 1 too many state variables. When the code is not correct (determined by my interaction with the react app), and I prompt the LLM with the bug + to fix it, it will almost always add complexity rather than rewrite parts of what it already had
────────
[4/11] another problem with LLMs as SWEs is that they don’t know when to refactor. a good example of this is when using react contexts vs hooks. When you instruct LLMs what to do, they don’t have the forward-looking vision of the app that you have, and it’s almost always more optimal to simply add one more piece of state to the context than refactor into hook(s)
────────
[5/11] a couple of times I’ve gotten burned by shipping LLM-generated code that passed my (few) interactions & receiving several bug complaints. It’s so hard to isolate bugs in clunky code that no human would have written in the first place (because it’s the composition of multiple broken diffs, and humans don’t generally keep around broken diffs)
────────
[6/11] Re: testing the wrong things—if i don’t tell an LLM what to test, it will write tests for the most complex features in my codebase. For example, if I have a feature that fits a logistic regression model to some data, the LLM will write tests for that first, even if my codebase function simply uses sklearn under the hood. There is no value in a test for a sklearn wrapper. I want LLMs to test features in my codebase that are likely to have implementation mistakes, even if they are very simple features, but this is far beyond even SOTA LLMs’ capability right now
────────
[7/11] a third problem (for me) is that LLMs write useless documentation & test the wrong things. whenever the LLM makes some complicated diff, i need documentation that is a mental model for what new logic lives where & a summary of how each new component works (specific to the programming language). I don’t care for inline comments or docstrings that much; what good is it to have doc strings when you cannot find the functions in the first place? Also LLM-generated docstrings are more imperative (explaining how the function works) than conceptual (the function’s role in the bigger system and why). Perhaps I should do more prompt engineering for my cursorrules
────────
[8/11] this thread ended up being more of a rant of problems in LLM-generated code, partially motivated by the fact that my X feed (startups, big cos, VCs, engineers, even professors) constantly shills LLMs-as-coders without any real discussion of real pain points
────────
[9/11] The heuristics I use for likely to have implementation mistakes are: the component accepts many types/categories of inputs that are not well-defined, and the component has high variance in its runtime. But these are very difficult heuristics to “teach” via in context learning
────────
[10/11] anyways, given the engagement trends here recently, I suspect nobody will see this thread. But I do hope I’m not alone in these thoughts
────────
[11/11] (caveat: AI-generated code is not my research area) I’ve talked about this to a few people and they say “ah a startup will solve it” or “it’s an engineering issue” but it’s really not. If you train people on isolated code snippets, you don’t get engineers. Training LLMs to be engineers requires some thoughtful supervision. Perhaps there’s a gross misunderstanding of what software engineering is. It’s not just programming

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] Our prompt engineering interface for DocETL supports branching, but it's not a chat anymore because branching + chat UI looks clunky (as echoed by some of the comments). We only render the LLM's last message. Branch names are user messages or summaries of user messages (cont.)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GgJM4ivXUAA5Lid.jpg
Quoting @samhogan
LLM chat interfaces need to support "branching" so it's possible to create a new thread with the *current* chat context to ask tertiary questions without polluting the context of future questions
────────
[2/6] I liked Sam's post and totally agree. During user studies we realized; it's not that users want to explore different threads in parallel, it's that users want to explore different threads *independently*. They don't have n independent ideas at once; they have an offshoot idea that they want to be able to try to see if it's the right path/way of thinking, but at no cost to future messages. In other words, without branching, users have to commit to the train of thought that arises from whatever message they are going to send, which can be limiting
────────
[3/6] Re: branching in chat looking bad: we also have a chat interface in DocETL. Initially I wanted our chat UI to enable users to "fork" the thread from earlier messages, akin to the Fork It UI for computational notebooks (Weinman et al. CHI 2021), with guided backtracking affordances. But, I got stuck trying to design the backtracking guidance. I also realized it was a bit clunky for users to have to consciously "fork"--in computational notebooks, people often have more clear ideas of what they want to do (e.g., try a different model architecture, different set of features), but in AI chats, many messages are loose and open-ended, often ambiguous
────────
[4/6] Moreover, it doesn't really make sense to fork at an AI's turn; only a user's turn (so you can try variations of the user message in that turn). Fortunately, that limits the space of possible forks. And users are way less likely to fork in the earliest turns; it might juts be simpler to restart the conversation with a better prompt that reflects the knowledge gained from the dead-end conversation
────────
[5/6] So ultimately, we ended up just designing an interface specifically for prompt engineering, outside of the chat interface, that displays the last message, and maintains a revision tree (the screenshot in my first/original tweet). Revisions are associated with user messages and store the chat history up until that point, though the entire chat history is not displayed. When the user clicks on a revision, they see the last AI message corresponding to that revision. It's pretty simple to be honest
────────
[6/6] Every now and then I look around for cool interface inspo, and haven't yet come across anything with chat + revision history. But I'm sure someone will figure it out!

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
been thinking about writing a blog post about this. my take is that it’s a mess of the following:
- if the goal is to minimize the time to working prototype, the framework will try to pydantic-ify or dataclass-ify everything (eg decorators for tools, memory objects)
- validation is not a first class citizen; usually (incorrectly treated as) an afterthought. maybe this is a consequence of the previous point, because simple LLM wrappers get you 90% of the way there
- validation needs to be hierarchical. for example, the first failure may result in a retry, the second may try a different prompt, the third may resort to a hard-coded fallback
- design patterns are implemented in agent frameworks as features (eg retries), so these frameworks seem like a hodgepodge of features
- people want to build agentic systems with a microservices mentality but this is a bad idea
- if there’s no UI/playground, there’s no easy way to iterate. iteration is required because nobody knows what the LLM is capable of until they try some prompts/agents
- minimal support for parallelization (a basic requirement)…users are left to reason about where and how to parallelize
- no support for progressively executing queries, ie where you return some results fast but keep running and slowly returning better results
will keep thinking about it and write something if I have anything new to add to the conversation
Quoting @abacaj
agent frameworks are useless (why are there so many)

Current data systems approach LLMs passively—treating them as costly black boxes operating on inputs as given, similar to expensive UDFs alongside relational operators. Wrangling prompts is the most frustrating part of building AI tools right now.
The user should be able to say "Yes, this was accurate", "This response wasn't good", or "I would have phrased it like this..."
The AI should then be allowed to edit its own prompt or include these examples as fine-tuning data. Too often, cramming the examples into the context window seems to confuse the model.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
putting my HCI hat on—
1. “semantic explode” is a brand new operator for data processing systems. desiderata for this operator are interesting: the generated outputs for the same key should be “sufficiently diverse,” and perhaps only the user/human can define “sufficiently diverse.”
2. interfaces to validate and steer “sufficiently diverse” (across groups of documents) are different from the row-by-row feedback interfaces that the HCI-evals subcommunities are building.
3. entity resolution and clustering interfaces are most closely related, but we’ve worked on it for decades and it’s still very hard to build something intuitive and useful.
4. (not HCI) optimizing the semantic explode operator will be tricky. it limits parallelism to have one output depend on others.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
a nice lens to reason about the complexity of LLM-powered data processing tasks
Quoting @jxmnop
# A new type of information theory
this paper is not super well-known but has changed my opinion of how deep learning works more than almost anything else
it says that we should measure the amount of information available in some representation based on how *extractable* it is, given finite computation. for example, an encrypted text file has less V-information than the same data in plaintext, because it takes more computation to extract. note the contrast to traditional information theory, which would tell us that the two representations have the same amount of Shannon information
i’ve long wondered why certain types of basic questions didn’t have a proper theoretical answer:
> why does distillation outperform vanilla maximum likelihood training?
> why does lora work better than finetuning?
> why does self-attention work better than almost any other similar operation?
> how much “information” remains in a text embedding?
> how much “information” remains in language model weights?
> should i use fine-tuning or RAG?
the true answers to all these questions depend on some way of measuring and comparing *information content* between different representations. v-information is one step towards doing this
besides computational constraints, model architecture probably affects the “information content” in representations, along with the presence of any pretraining data used, as well as model-level statistics about the optimization in the training process – e.g. the length of time a model was trained for probably changes representations pretty drastically
this is all to say, i think there is some true notion of “information” that none of our current paradigms (Shannon information, V-information, etc.) capture. we encounter this idea every day but we dance around it and describe it in vague terms; we measure it from all sorts of angles but can’t quite characterize it theoretically
when the v-information paper came out I thought there would be a lot of follow up work developing more complex and useful notions of information for deep learning. but it hasn’t
yet I still think at the heart of these questions of what-information-lies-in-representations there’s something to be found that’s profound, elegant, and potentially extremely useful. I don’t know what it is and i’m probably not the person who will figure it out. but I really hope someone does. :)

[1/2] we’re teaching a course for engineers and technical PMs on evals for AI products! why?
despite all the tooling out there, there’s very little *education* on how to build evals—like, what’s the actual process from vague idea to deployed product? how do you know if your system is good? what does “good” even mean? what processes does one follow?

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] ⭐new MLOps preprint⭐
RAG is everywhere, but building RAG is still painful. When something breaks--the retriever? the LLM?--developers are left guessing, & iterating is often slow
we built a better way & used it as a design probe to study expert workflows 👇
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GpUK41FbAAA1jJG.jpg
────────
[2/6] Meet raggy: an interactive debugging interface for RAG pipelines. It pairs a Python library of RAG primitives with a UI that lets devs inspect, edit, & rerun steps in real time. raggy precomputes many indexes for retrieval upfront, so you can easily swap them out when debugging!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GpUK9ucbYAYCkXy.jpg
────────
[3/6] so what are some takeaways?
- vector DBs and RAG tooling should build special interfaces ("playgrounds") that allow users to explore various retrieval methods, indexes, and how these integrate with the end-to-end LLM pipeline
- devs need better support for creating eval sets as they are iterating and debugging!
- like traditional MLOps, devs may benefit from assistance in finding what components to trace errors back to
────────
[4/6] Then, to learn more about expert workflows, we ran a study with 12 engineers who’ve built production RAG pipelines. We simulated a question-answering application from a hospital & watched our participants use raggy to build and iterate on their pipelines. The paper reports a bunch of qualitative findings, including:
🔍 They always debug retrieval first
⚙️ Fixes to one step often break another
⚡ Fast iteration was key: raggy turned half-day experiments into seconds!!
────────
[5/6] "RAG without the lag" is part of a broader MLOps agenda in our research group: making ML pipelines easier to build, debug, and trust.
Work led by Quentin Romero Lauro (who did an REU with us)--who will be applying for PhD programs next year!
Was a very fun collaboration with @Qromerolauro, @SepantaZeighami, @adityagp
Do reach out if you are interested in us giving a talk on this work at your org or group!

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (6 tweets)
summary:
[1/6] We have a paper to appear at NAACL this week: PromptEvals! ✨
In collaboration with LangChain, we release a dataset of 2k+ developer-written LLM prompts and 12k+ assertion criteria: 5× larger than prior collections; plus open-source models 🛠️ to automatically generate assertion criteria
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gpo9gmdbEAAAofP.jpg
────────
[2/6] So we collected and cleaned real-world prompts.
For each prompt, we generated assertion criteria, or specific checks derived from the prompt’s instructions, grounded in taxonomies from prior work.
These assertions capture what production LLM evals actually look like.
────────
[3/6] As we were building evals tooling and doing research, we realized: there’s almost no data on what prompts real developers write---or what behaviors they actually care about checking.
Without this data, it was difficult to systematically design reliable evaluation methods.
────────
[4/6] This work was led by Reya Vir (@ReyaVir ), who will be starting her PhD at Columbia this fall! 🎓
She’ll be presenting it at NAACL---please reach out if you’re there!
Paper:
Datasets and models can be found here:
And of course, the paper would not be possible without the help and guidance from @hwchase17 @WHinthorn @langchain @adityagp
────────
[5/6] We also fine-tuned 7B and 8B models (Mistral and Llama 3) to automatically generate assertion criteria.
Our models beat GPT-4o by 20.9% on average F1, while being much cheaper and faster to run. 🚀
All models and datasets are open-sourced!
Full benchmark + HuggingFace links in the paper. 📚
────────
[6/6] Why assertions? Most evals in production are actually operationalized through assertions:
✅ Check if the output satisfies a constraint (format, groundedness, tone, etc.)
✅ If not, flag, retry, or reject
PromptEvals gives the first large-scale dataset to learn and benchmark this process.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] This is a really good question. In my experience, domain experts' reluctance to write prompts boils down to
- not knowing how to write a good prompt in the first place (it's not necessarily as simple as instructing a human expert/coworker to do the task)
- not having the iterative loop/feedback cycle to understand how their prompt performed
Here is my advice
1. Teach them the structure of a good prompt, so they know what *you* (as the eng/dev/PM) are looking for. See screenshot attached. you don't have to use terminology like "few-shot prompting" but giving this four-part formula can be really helpful for them
2. "Ease in" their involvement slowly. Perhaps have them dictate a first version of the prompt, following a formula. Then have them review pipeline outputs (rather than get them to write revisions of the prompt). This will build intuition for strengths and weaknesses of LLMs, pin some good examples to use as few-shot examples in the prompt, and perhaps clarify instructions even more (i.e., make them less ambiguous)
3. Build good interfaces for domain experts. Interfaces for reviewing outputs, for testing variations of the prompts on a sample, etc.
4. Domain experts are more down to edit prompts / propose edits / review edits to prompts than write them in the first place. it is really hard to write something from scratch
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GqXgagaa0AE1uYb.png
Quoting @verrsane
We always talk about having the domain expert writing their own prompts
But some of my clients don’t want to write the prompts, they want me to do it
How do I teach domain experts how to write prompts and encourage them to do so for our projects?
────────
[2/2] I am not a natural at marketing/sales but I have to say: take our course to read the entire book and hear about examples of how we did this
we have a chapter dedicated to collaborative labeling and evaluation, and another chapter dedicated to eval interface design.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Some tips for LLM/agent pipeline design to maximize prefix sharing
- if only one LLM call (no data reuse), put instructions before data in prompt to benefit from caching
- if there is data reuse (ie 2+ LLM calls operation on the same data or document) and the size of the data is greater than the size of the task instruction, put the data before any fine grained task instructions
- if your task instructions are placed first in the prompt, fire one call for the LLM step before executing other LLM calls in parallel (so there’s something in the cache to hit)
- if there is data reuse, generic/repeatable instructions can go before the data. Eg you can say “you are legal expert helping me find and reason about clauses in contracts” to “ground” your agents (seems to be a magic prompt optimization trick)
These tricks are especially relevant for LLM as judge pipelines, where you often have lots of data reuse (because you want to judge different qualities of the output)

summary:
This was a fun talk to give, and even more fun to talk to many attendees afterwards. The gist was that people mostly skip to improving generalization of **well-specificed** prompts and pipelines to different inputs & data...before having well-specified prompts & agents in the first place. Do the work to (1) deeply understand your data and task through experimenting with agent outputs (i.e., figure out what criteria to evaluate), (2) specify your pipelines as well as possible, then (3) pull out the fun tricks like prompt optimization, task decomposition, RL, fine-tuning, etc.
Quoting @LangChain

- Many failure modes around data understanding, evals must be task specific
- Intent gap between that the user asks and what they want. DocETL uses human feedback to align to this over time
- "You're never just 'done' with evals... failures hide in the long tail"

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] this three gulfs mental model came from a recent paper submission I haven't posted about yet. I will post about it later, but here I want to reflect on the three gulfs model, and how lovely it feels to be able to translate HCI-AI ideas into practice to have ~impact~.
one of the reasons why LLM application developers find their job so challenging is because they have to wear different hats all the time--data science hat to **comprehend** the data; PM & communication hat to **specify** a good prompt, and eng hat to **generalize** their prompts to production data (e.g., use more powerful models, automated prompt engineering to find good few shot examples, fine tune or RLHF, decompose into multiple smaller tasks, etc.)
people often mistake specification issues for generalization issues (or vice versa), or try to tackle two gulfs without considering the third. to build truly effective products, you have to bridge all the gulfs, and build the bridges anew for pretty much any application. you also have to recognize, when your process feels in a slump, what gulf you are in---so you can put on the right hat and unblock yourself.
it's awesome that the three gulfs model resonated a lot with Hamel and Eugene---experts who have helped hundreds of teams ship strong LLM applications. we are presenting it in our evals book, and I think it will slowly, over the next year, go on to be a very useful mental model for LLM application developers
Quoting @HamelHusain
The three gulfs of LLM pipeline development is a powerful mental model to keep in mind while creating AI evals.
@eugeneyan , @sh_reya and I discuss here (links to more resources in the replies)
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1923382183768866816/img/5w57P_WrlD4JDvzJ.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1923382183768866816/vid/avc1/320x320/8tLuhCqvgimpkel-.mp4?tag=14

When I started my PhD, I simply wanted to learn more about the rich history of computing systems & build cool things. I did not realize I would learn things that would position me to build useful systems and understand humans and developers better given today's technologies (e.g., LLMs, cheap and fast cloud services). impact comes in many forms (e.g., systems, influencing others' systems, books/education) and can take a long time to realize. I feel like all my collaborators and I are only 1% of the way into this journey, and I am really excited for the road ahead

- compute, memory, and disk reqs for diff model sizes

Is this the right idea? or should we have a kitchen sink of reward functions and remove rewards that are easily hackable after inspecting outputs? also should we be thinking about adaptive rewards based on the step?

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] folks have been asking about the behind the scenes
- I use cursor. I've tried replit and like it as well (screenshots in my evals course reader are from replit, actually) but I find that it's more helpful to have the vibe-coded app be an evolving artifact in my experimentation codebase
- I ask for fastapi + HTML (javascript allowed as well). no react or other web dev frameworks. no dependencies for me to install (put the bundles in the html). I want the whole thing to be executable from a python file like "python run_app.py", so the main function basically is just uvicorn . run.
- I also ask for hotkeys and auto-saving functionality (write my open codes or notes to a csv)
- I ALWAYS ask for a theme or vibe. e.g., "sleek terminal theme" or "minimal text, just headers and hotkeys" or "minimal roundness." sometimes I have tried "windows XP theme" and that's also fun.
- if you don't ask for a theme or vibe, you get ugly defaults! Claude's default is to give you way too many colors with very rounded cards and a single left or top border for each card. Gemini 2.5 pro loves extra-nested cards. o3 is too expensive for me to try too much, lol.
- after playing around with the first version of my interface I usually also vibe code a search interface that allows me to click on any trace I'm inspecting & search for the nearest neighbor successful and failure traces
- these vibe coded apps die after I've graduated from the project (e.g., moved onto next experiment or built an entirely new version of the pipeline). they are meant to be ephemeral imo
