title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
I am forever on the soapbox of build custom and domain specific LLM output grading interfaces. But more recently, I’ve become interested in mental models of LLM behavior for domain (not AI) experts. While it may seem strange to an AI expert to have a “add domain knowledge” button, because one cannot know the impact of clicking the button (eg cannot possibly know if, definitively, the LLM was trained on the knowledge or not, or what all is in the prompt/context, or, how specifying the facts will actually influence model behavior): the “add domain knowledge” suggests that people may find it easier to think of the AI as an entity with “gaps” in knowledge that need to be filled, and the human role is then to fill these gaps
Quoting @ChrisLovejoy_
Building a dashboard for domain experts to review AI outputs is critical for domain-specific LLM apps.
Principles we followed at @AnteriorAI when building ours:
(1) Optimise for providing all relevant context as intuitively as possible
Our doctors and nurses say the hardest part of reviewing AI outputs is getting the same context the AI has.
Our interface makes the medical record and guideline document accessible on right hand side with the AI outputs laid out on the left, providing clear mental separation.
(2) Design the user review flow from first principles, not their existing workflows
Different domain experts develop their own workflow over time through habit.
Our opinion is that there is an 'ideal' workflow which you can guide them towards, optimising for both speed and accuracy.
(3) Don't just get correctness, get failure modes and suggested fixes at the same time
You want your reviews to help you improve your system, not just tell you how you're doing.
Measuring multiple things at once prevents your domain experts from needing to keep re-loading context for an AI output.
In our dashboard, you can see 'correct/incorrect', 'add domain knowledge' and 'tag failure mode'.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GusygcDXAAA67bu.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (5 tweets)
summary:
[1/5] thoughts on background coding agents (form factor; inferring developer intent)
────────
[2/5] form factor
i was initially skeptical that an agent decoupled from an IDE would be useful. however i realized that there are several non-critical issues in my repos that would be nice to fix, but i would never have time to do (each would take ~1-2 hours). these kinds of tasks are natural to delegate to a background agent; i don't have to keep any workspace or tab open. i just submit the prompts and close the tabs; revisiting whenever i have time. i especially like that if the fix looks good, i can automatically create a PR
────────
[3/5] inferring developer intent (cont.)
.cursorrules are surprisingly unhelpful--i realize i wrote many of my .cursorrules for foreground agents; where i *want* to be in the loop more, but for background agents, i want the agent to make minimal changes yet still infer as much as possible, even if i did not precisely specify my intent.
────────
[4/5] form factor (cont.)
background agents work best when they write their own tests and CI (which runs on PR for me) passes, and when i skim the diff, i find nothing too fishy. however it is extremely clunky to have to make _any_ change to the PR. in other words, switching between background and foreground agents is really annoying. if i check out the PR in cursor or VSCode, it does not have the chat history that the background agent has, so i'm forced to give a bunch of context on what the PR introduced, what the bug might be, and what i want changed. i find it easier to just make the fixes myself in the PR. the experience is like reviewing a really bad junior engineer's PR and fixing the code myself as a learning experience / demonstration.
────────
[5/5] inferring developer intent (cont.)
i would never give a background agent a poorly scoped or super underspecified task. however, i frequently give such tasks to foreground agents, since i expect to read the chain of thoughts and steer the direction of the code. it feels strange to me that there's no "onboarding" to teach me how to use a background agent, and whether my invocation was "successful." it feels even more strange that the foreground and background agents are presented in largely similar ways

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] Extraction isn't the biggest need in document analysis; it's what you need to do after extraction. We are finding that many analysis tasks involve sorting documents by nuanced, human-centric qualities. E.g., "Which contracts are most risky? Which medical reports are most urgent? Which support tickets are the least spammy? How does the language or tone differ as you move up or down the axis you are sorting along?"
But you can't just dump 1,000s of documents into an LLM and hope for a good ordering. That's where DocETL pipelines come in. So we made a real-world example:
We used DocETL to semantically rank 179 lease contracts by how severe their "red flags" are for lessees (fully automatic, $4.24 total cost):
Step 1⃣: Extract and summarize every red-flag clause (uncapped fees, harsh penalties, etc.) using an LLM
Step 2⃣: Rank each contract by how dangerous those flags are
This map → rank pattern works for almost any domain—finance, law, health, ops—anywhere you need to triage or prioritize docs before reading.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GxhNCyMasAAveij.jpg
────────

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
The first thing you learn as a Berkeley DB PhD student is that pervasive & successful software systems are rarely one-size-fits-all. The relational database is a great example. Everyone uses one. On the interface side: not everyone needs the same isolation levels, transactions, consistency guarantees, etc. On the systems side: the more we know about a workload, the better we can optimize it. For AI models, analogous interface primitives are only recently emerging, like “reasoning” budgets and memory. And we are also only recently starting to learn about the common workloads, e.g., coding, long context, Q&A or retrieval, writing.
Quoting @Yuchenj_UW
ChatGPT users are canceling subscriptions.
GPT-5 as the main source of intelligence does not work.
Intelligence isn’t one-size-fits-all; user needs and preferences vary wildly. We want more models. We want more control.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/Gx66SXWbgAAOEOF.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (3 tweets)
summary:
[1/3] From DocETL users, we’ve noticed another common unstructured data analysis pattern: filter → label (i.e., map) → aggregate.
For example, I pulled ~1,000 congressional commerce hearing transcripts, filtered for public health, then had DocETL:
1⃣ Label the most "quotable" moments + tone (adversarial, empathetic, evasive) and role (member, chair, witness)
2⃣ Aggregate per-hearing stats like evasion rate, top topics, and most quotable lines
Interestingly, this pipeline started as just 2–3 operators, but grew to 7 as I explored the data and realized more layers of reasoning I wanted to capture. (Along the way I learned things like, what Narcan doesn't respond to, post-incarceration overdose risks, and from the FDA commissioner: "In God we trust, all others must bring data" lol)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GyF2WAOaEAUWINd.jpg

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
I have an unpopular opinion. Claude code in my terminal is a far superior experience to the equivalent model (even in max mode) in Cursor agent mode. Here’s what I do in my IDE that I don’t do with Claude code
- i write underspecified prompts and instructions because I have the illusion it is easy to correct any mistakes that arise with a follow up message later
- i stay in the editor watching the agent think. Absolute waste of my time. It is better to batch my prompting labor upfront so I can do other tasks as the agent keeps thinking and writing
- i let conversations grow to 20+ messages; the quality degrades and i get very frustrated
- i feel motivated to code other things in the project as the agent is working, and i inevitably run into conflicts esp if I have to roll back agent changes. When the code is the main part of the window, I inevitably think that code is the most important artifact of the project. Which is false. Clear thinking & specifications are the most important artifacts of any modern software projects
When I am using cursor agent, I actively try to avoid my bad behaviors. But it is hard. The agentic IDE gives me too much leeway and lets me “defer” clear thinking until later stages in my project. The main issue is that I don’t always know when I am not thinking clearly enough. To use the cursor agent effectively, I have to actively wonder, “would I have said this any differently to Claude code? A collaborator? What am I missing?” And it’s too much work
Quoting @svpino
I can’t believe I have to be the one saying this:
An IDE for software development is better than a command line interface.
We fought this war and won it a long time ago.
Why is now every model provider releasing a CLI for AI coding?
What’s this madness about?

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] Our first DocETL paper has been accepted to VLDB 2025! DocETL is a system we’ve been building at Berkeley for reliable LLM-powered data pipelines, where the optimizer logically rewrites pipelines because even experts cannot author one that is accurate enough to begin with.
I'll be presenting it at VLDB in a couple weeks. And because database papers rarely get traction on social media, I always like to give the backstory — in hopes that the story is fun or resonates more broadly. 😃
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/GypuJxAbgAAofoX.jpg
────────
[2/9] In early 2023, LLM APIs were just starting to take off. We knew they were going to be important building blocks in next-generation data systems, but we didn’t know how. And as a researcher, there’s no better way to find out than to roll up your sleeves and try solving real problems yourself. The first problem I tried came from a college friend. They had endless customer support logs and wanted a running summary of pain points to know what bugs to fix. Naively, I dumped everything into GPT-4 and asked for a summary. It looked polished, but it missed the actual recurring issues and never pulled reliable quotes.
────────
[3/9] What struck us was that these weren't prompt-engineering problems. They were structural decomposition problems. Every serious task required breaking down into sub-task, where, crucially, each sub-task is something that an LLM can reliably do. But even expert engineers couldn’t predict the right decomposition without long cycles of trial and error. This is what makes LLM pipelines different from SQL.
In a database, users declare what they want, and the optimizer finds a good plan. We can assume the query itself is correct. For LLMs, we can’t even write a pipeline that works "as is" on state-of-the-art models. So the optimizer must generate and test different pipelines on the user’s behalf. Optimizers need to test many different logical rewrites of the initial pipeline to see what will work best.
────────
[4/9] Around the same time, coauthors in Berkeley's EPIC Lab were working on police misconduct records. They wanted to extract instances of misconduct (e.g., excessive use of force) and other structured information from these records. They faced the same pattern at a larger scale: LLM steps seemed to fail, so they kept rewriting pipelines — chunking documents, appending context, summarizing, introducing sub-pipelines — for months.
────────
[5/9] So I started tinkering. I built pipelines: one LLM call per log to extract quotes and classify the log, then a second call to write a global summary with a very detailed prompt. But each step was fragile. I spent more time rewriting taxonomies, prompts, and chunking strategies than writing the code to orchestrate the LLM calls. So the hard part wasn't the system; it was designing the pipeline itself.
────────
[6/9] On the Berkeley police misconduct dataset, DocETL’s optimizer automatically discovered pipelines that doubled recall compared to a strong human-engineered baseline. Pipelines that would have taken experts weeks of tinkering emerged automatically from the search. We are pretty bullish on agentic rewriting and optimization; as LLMs get better and we design more efficient search algorithms to find better pipelines, hopefully one day we author very simple pipelines and hand them off to the agent to cook up the best pipeline for us.
So ultimately, what began as two parallel frustrations turned into a year-long, multi-lab research effort. Along the way, the project grew well beyond anything I could have hoped. DocETL is now open source, with collaborators across Berkeley and beyond, and multiple follow-on papers already accepted or in progress
────────
[7/9] So over the year we built DocETL: a system that lets users author pipelines of LLM-powered operators, with an optimizer that rewrites those pipelines top-down. Given a library of 13 open-ended rewrite directives — guidelines for how to logically decompose a pipeline — the optimizer uses LLM agents to instantiate these rewrites and to synthesize task-specific criteria for evaluating outputs, ultimately selecting the most accurate pipeline.
────────
[8/9] I’ll be presenting the paper on Tuesday, Sep 2 at VLDB. You can read it at Follow along with the open source project at and This first paper was a super fun collaboration with Tristan, Tarak, Eugene, and my advisor Aditya
And: I’m also going on the CS faculty job market this cycle — if your department is hiring and you’re interested in the DocETL line of work, please reach out!
────────
[9/9] For me, DocETL has been more than a lesson in how to build reliable AI-powered data systems. Bigger models aren’t enough; reliability comes from structuring tasks into pipelines, and from optimizers that can invent, rewrite, and validate those pipelines for us. But the DocETL project has also given me a clearer picture of how LLMs will transform data systems more broadly: what new applications are possible, how end users will create them on the fly, and how we should rethink AI-powered application development beyond data systems. It's even shaped how I teach AI and data engineering.
As the AI community keeps building more powerful models, it's up to us in systems research to figure out how to architect around those building blocks. That excites me at every level — from the deep technical challenges, to the larger sociotechnical questions of how these systems integrate into society, and how data-centric workflows across industries will be redesigned to optimally allocate work between humans and AI.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
One of the most pressing questions in our AI Evals course is: "Why can’t I just have an LLM write my LLM pipeline?" The nuanced answer is that you can use LLMs to assist, but not for the whole pipeline. Knowing where to put the LLM in the loop is the hard part.
To unpack this, we invited Omar Khattab (@lateinteraction) —creator of DSPy, leading expert on prompt optimization, and now professor at MIT—for a "fireside chat" in the course. He shed light on how he approaches pipeline development in practice. What stood out to us is that Omar spends most of his time on specification—e.g., defining the task clearly, looking at the data, and doing careful error analysis—before letting LLMs automate anything. This up-front rigor is what makes downstream optimization actually work.
We've put the recording on YouTube. If you're wondering how Omar thinks about these tradeoffs, this conversation is worth a listen!

[1/3] I spent a lot of time early in the PhD learning how to do user studies (and qualitative methods more generally). It has surprisingly been very valuable for my career as a data systems researcher. I highly recommend first and second year CS PhD students take an HCI methods class
Quoting @vishal_learner
Also, would love to see these types of small user studies more widespread in ML papers or even blog posts. How cool would it be to read about how 5 ML researchers used your new model/training recipe/dataset/library/etc and what their experience was
────────
[2/3] Why do user studies as a systems researcher? User studies are a tool to teach you something new and important about your research vision, that will seed or change the way you approach aspects of your future work
────────
[3/3] Should you always do user studies in every paper? No! Sometimes you have a research question that can be answered with some other methodology. Sometimes you can have papers centered around a user study evaluation; sometimes user studies can be one of multiple evaluations; sometimes you don’t need user studies

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Our paper "Steering Semantic Data Processing with DocWrangler" will be receiving a Best Paper Honorable Mention in a couple of weeks at UIST 2025!
DocWrangler is a mixed-initiative IDE we built at Berkeley for semantic data processing, where users work with AI to analyze unstructured documents. It addresses the following challenge: even with LLMs, writing effective data pipelines requires constant back-and-forth between understanding your data and expressing what you want.
I will give the backstory in this thread, in hopes that folks will be motivated to read the paper :-)
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G051dZwbIAIXXZM.jpg
────────
[2/8] We came to the DocWrangler problem after building DocETL, our declarative system for optimizing and executing LLM-powered data processing pipelines. People vaguely knew what they wanted to extract and transform, but they didn't really know how to specify it.
────────
[3/8] This isn't just about phrasing things so an LLM can follow instructions. The process of writing and running the pipeline forces you to clarify your own intent. You write down a prompt, look at the outputs, and only then realize—"wait, I don't want the symptoms the doctor mentioned, I want the ones the patient reported."
────────
[4/8] For example: suppose you want to "extract symptoms from medical conversation transcripts." That sounds straightforward, but the moment you try, you realize you don’t actually know what you want. Does "symptom" mean what the patient currently has, or what they had in the past? Do you include side effects from medications? Do you only care about severe ones?
────────
[5/8] I am especially proud that the three gulfs model has resonated well beyond semantic data processing—it has shaped how people think about AI pipeline development more generally, and it is now part of the curriculum for the course "AI Evals for Engineers and PMs," which is also being adopted in ~5 different university courses this fall.
────────
[6/8] DocWrangler is our attempt to address these gulfs directly. We built features like in-situ notes to help with comprehension, model-assisted prompt refinement to help with specification, and operation decomposition to help with generalization. We then ran user studies to see how analysts actually made progress with DocWrangler, and followed that with an online deployment with over 1500 uses that revealed the kinds of pipelines people really author in practice. You should read the paper for the full set of insights, and I'll also link below to some great threads from others who have written about our findings.
────────
[7/8] We started to see the same challenges come up again and again, through different examples. We called them the Three Gulfs.
- The gulf of comprehension: users struggle to make sense of long, messy documents and spot what matters.
- The gulf of specification: even when they know what they want, it’s hard to express precisely in a prompt.
- The gulf of generalization: pipelines that work on one small set of documents often don't work on the next, because LLMs are error-prone.
────────
[8/8] Overall, this was a really fun collaboration with folks across data systems, HCI, and AI. Looking forward, I'm excited for the next generation of data systems that won't just execute our specifications; they'll help us discover what we actually want to know; more like partners in sensemaking, not just tools for execution.
If you work with messy documents, need to extract insights at scale, or just want to see what human-AI collaboration for data analysis looks like, try DocWrangler at (and check out the repo at
Read our paper at
And catch me at UIST giving this talk in a couple weeks! I am on the faculty job market this cycle :-)

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] 100% agree with Andrew on the unreasonable effectiveness of error analysis, and that it’s a bit different for genAI and agents. Turns out there is a structured & well established framework to help with error analysis in gen AI—grounded theory! Hamel and I go into detail and do live error analysis with a real agent in an episode on Lenny’s podcast that we recorded over the summer (link below)
Quoting @AndrewYNg
Readers responded with both surprise and agreement last week when I wrote that the single biggest predictor of how rapidly a team makes progress building an AI agent lay in their ability to drive a disciplined process for evals (measuring the system’s performance) and error analysis (identifying the causes of errors). It’s tempting to shortcut these processes and to quickly attempt fixes to mistakes rather than slowing down to identify the root causes. But evals and error analysis can lead to much faster progress. In this first of a two-part letter, I’ll share some best practices for finding and addressing issues in agentic systems.
Even though error analysis has long been an important part of building supervised learning systems, it is still underappreciated compared to, say, using the latest and buzziest tools. Identifying the root causes of particular kinds of errors might seem “boring,” but it pays off! If you are not yet persuaded that error analysis is important, permit me to point out:
- To master a composition on a musical instrument, you don’t only play the same piece from start to end. Instead, you identify where you’re stumbling and practice those parts more.
- To be healthy, you don’t just build your diet around the latest nutrition fads. You also ask your doctor about your bloodwork to see if anything is amiss. (I did this last month and am happy to report I’m in good health! 😃)
- To improve your sports team’s performance, you don’t just practice trick shots. Instead, you review game films to spot gaps and then address them.
To improve your agentic AI system, don’t just stack up the latest buzzy techniques that just went viral on social media (though I find it fun to experiment with buzzy AI techniques as much as the next person!). Instead, use error analysis to figure out where it’s falling short, and focus on that.
Before analyzing errors, we first have to decide what is an error. So the first step is to put in evals. I’ll focus on that for the remainder of this letter and discuss error analysis next week.
If you are using supervised learning to train a binary classifier, the number of ways the algorithm could make a mistake is limited. It could output 0 instead of 1, or vice versa. There is also a handful of standard metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC, etc. that apply to many problems. So as long as you know the test distribution, evals are relatively straightforward, and much of the work of error analysis lies in identifying what types of input an algorithm fails on, which also leads to data-centric AI techniques for acquiring more data to augment the algorithm in areas where it’s weak.
With generative AI, a lot of intuitions from evals and error analysis of supervised learning carry over — history doesn’t repeat itself, but it rhymes — and developers who are already familiar with machine learning and deep learning often adapt to generative AI faster than people who are starting from scratch. But one new challenge is that the space of outputs is much richer, so there are many more ways an algorithm’s output might be wrong.
Take the example of automated processing of financial invoices where we use an agentic workflow to populate a financial database with information from received invoices. Will the algorithm incorrectly extract the invoice due date? Or the final amount? Or mistake the payer address for the biller address? Or get the financial currency wrong? Or make the wrong API call so the verification process fails? Because the output space is much larger, the number of failure modes is also much larger.
Rather than defining an error metric ahead of time, it is therefore typically more effective to first quickly build a prototype, then manually examine a handful of agent outputs to see where it performs well and where it stumbles. This allows you to focus on building datasets and error metrics — sometimes objective metrics implemented in code, and sometimes subjective metrics using LLM-as-judge — to check the system’s performance in the dimensions you are most concerned about. In supervised learning, we sometimes tune the error metric to better reflect what humans care about. With agentic workflows, I find tuning evals to be even more iterative, with more frequent tweaks to the evals to capture the wider range of things that can go wrong.
I discuss this and other best practices in detail in Module 4 of the Agentic AI course on that we announced last week. After building evals, you now have a measurement of your system’s performance, which provides a foundation for trying different modifications to your agent, as you can now measure what makes a difference. The next step is then to perform error analysis to pinpoint what changes to focus your development efforts on. I’ll discuss this further next week.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] DocETL is a system we’ve been building at Berkeley for the past two years to make large-scale unstructured data analysis reliable and efficient. It powers our broader stack—used by journalists, public defenders, and researchers—to extract, transform, and reason over messy documents with LLMs.
As part of making the DocETL ecosystem easier to use, we’re introducing a natural language–to–pipeline generator! Our hosted version is free to use BUT we're collecting the data so we can build better tools.
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/1987946944258535424/img/ftimXnqTVo8EF0EC.jpg | https://video.twimg.com/amplify_video/1987946944258535424/vid/avc1/452x270/pBYomWe1TY7AcJnA.mp4?tag=21
────────
[2/4] DocETL (and the DocWrangler IDE) are both open-source; please give it a star at :-)
We have more papers coming out later this month (from the systems side) on efficient data processing; stay tuned!
────────
[3/4] Try it out at You have to upload a dataset in JSON or as a CSV; or you can upload individual documents via the file upload. We’d love to learn where it breaks and what new capabilities you want next!
────────
[4/4] Authoring DocETL pipelines from scratch can be tough: operators are defined on-the-fly in natural language, and users must bridge a “gulf of specification,” or figure out how to express their complex intent in natural language. Inspired by end-user programming, this prototype lets you describe your task without having to think about specific operators, generates a starting pipeline, runs it on sample data, and shows results immediately.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
I often find that this question leads to a more nuanced discussion. "Evals" or the evaluation process broadly consists of three components: (1) identifying the criteria, or rubric, for success, (2) determining how to apply the rubric to LLM outputs, and (3) doing 2, i.e., applying the rubric to outputs, at scale in an automated fashion. Let us walk through an example. For coding agents very broadly, (1) can consist of: compiling with no errors, executing with no errors, executing quickly, executing with the correct answer, and more. (2) can be quite straightforward if the criteria in (1) is very well-defined. In some highly subjective domains, (2) is tricky to come up with and requires a human to go through the process of applying the rubric to 100s of outputs to learn more about the problem. The "criteria drift" phenomenon in my UIST 2024 paper emerges in (2). But for coding agents i'll presume that (2) is quite simple because the metrics in (1) are well-defined, and there is no criteria drift. Then, (3) is about writing a function to apply the rubric & check correctness, and the "harness" needed to manage the function (e.g., manage state, sandbox environment). The function needs to be both sound and complete---"sound" meaning, correct and consistent at scale; "complete" meaning, the hypothetical universe of correctness indicators is covered by the function. For coding agents, (3) is often a containerized environment that can execute shell commands. If you have evals (all 3 of the above), you can work on (4) building the flywheel/training an agent to improve on these evals.
Now what is verifiability? In plain English, it's the ability to check whether something is correct. Under the framework above, verifiability is not a separate category of tasks; it's just the existence of some instantiation of (1)–(3) that correctly captures what "success" means. In that sense, all tasks are theoretically verifiable; the difficulty lies in constructing a workable rubric and evaluator. Some tasks admit obvious, objective instantiations (coding, math); others require much more human iteration to converge on criteria, uncover drift, or formalize subjective judgments. And even for tasks that seem "easily verifiable," multiple instantiations of steps (1)–(3) exist — from more strict unit tests to behavioral tests — each encoding a different definition of correctness. So verifiability isn’t binary. It's about whether one can articulate and automate a version of (1)–(3) that faithfully captures the notion of correctness you care about.
I get pretty confused by the twitter & arxiv discourse; when people mention that some tasks aren't verifiable. So maybe the implicit definition of verifiability the AI community seems to have is: how easily a task can be given clear criteria and an automated, trustworthy way to apply them — not whether verifiability is possible at all. Verifiability seems to be a property of the evaluation design space the researcher has created (i.e., how well they have specified and automated criteria).
Quoting @homerdev
@karpathy Is Verifiability == Evals?
The easier a task is to verify, the easier it is to scale the system with evals cc @HamelHusain @sh_reya

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
I really enjoyed giving this talk!!
Quoting @HamelHusain
New video from @sh_reya on data processing with LLMs at scale, an underrated topic!
Shreya starts with a real use case: public defenders analyzing case files for racial bias (4:08). Hundreds of pages per defendant. Court transcripts, police reports, news articles. Running GPT-5 on everything costs a fortune.
Her solution: treat LLMs like database operators. Semantic Map, Filter, Reduce (9:18). Databricks, BigQuery, and Snowflake are already shipping this as "AI SQL." She discusses how starting at 12:51: a query optimizer for LLMs.
Traditional databases rewrite queries for efficiency. Shreya does the same for LLM pipelines (semantic versions of split, map, reduce that are LLM specific, along with query decomposition). For example, trivial LLM calls are replaced with Python functions.
These "rewrite directives" improve both cost AND accuracy.
She also talks about a cost optimization technique: Task Cascades (30:00).
Instead of running GPT-5 on every document, first ask cheap questions. "Is there any lower court mentioned?" If no, the document clearly doesn't overturn a lower court. There are many other routing questions you can ask to reduce the amount of text sent to the LLM. This requires careful optimization and tuning to get right. She explains how to do this in the video.
She runs through a production example that achieved 86% cost reduction while retaining 90% accuracy.
---
At 41:26, Shreya shifts to HCI. She built DocWrangler, an IDE for LLM pipelines. The design is based on "Three Gulfs" (44:35):
1. Comprehension: You don't know what's in your data
2. Specification: "Only prescription meds" is hard to operationalize
3. Generalization: A prompt that works on 10 examples fails at 10,000
Users invented "throwaway pipelines" just to explore their data before doing real analysis. Pipelines with no analytical purpose: "summarize these documents," "extract key ideas." Just ways to learn what's in their data before doing the real work. DocWrangler makes this a first-class feature.
---
In the last bit of the video Shreya discusses why you can't know what "good" means until you see examples.
In one study, a medical analyst extracted medications from doctor-patient transcripts. As they inspected outputs, they noticed every medication appeared with a dosage. They hadn't anticipated this. Now they wanted dosages too. They also saw Tylenol and ibuprofen appearing and realized: "Actually, I only want prescription medications."
Shreya calls this "criteria drift." Your evaluation criteria evolve as you see more outputs. This matters because standard ML assumes fixed metrics: define them upfront, collect labels, measure. But with LLMs on fuzzy tasks, that assumption breaks. You discover what you actually want through the process of evaluating.
If you don't account for criteria drift, you end up optimizing for a stale rubric. DocWrangler and EvalGen accommodate this by placing the human in the loop thoughtfully.
Chapter timestamps:
(4:08) - The problem: unstructured data at scale
(9:18) - Semantic operators (Map, Filter, Reduce)
(12:51) - Query optimization for LLMs
(18:15) - Data decomposition (chunking)
(30:00) - Task Cascades (86% cost reduction)
(41:26) - DocWrangler IDE
(44:35) - Three Gulfs framework
(51:50) - Evaluation criteria drift

Anyways, I’ve started to put together a personal eval suite that I can run at any time. Since I’m not testing the API endpoints (I’m just testing the web apps and cursor and Claude code), the scaffold is a bit wonky. I manually run the query a couple of times and save the outputs. There are also too many confounding factors (eg chatgpt/claude memory impacting subsequent runs of the same query). My eval suite is small: one document extraction task; one abstract writing task (based on my paper and a list of writing guidelines); one task that generates a comment on a research abstract (based on some bullet points from me); one task that generates a DocETL pipeline; one task that plans out a 3 day trip with restaurants that satisfy my dietary restrictions. I often don’t run all of them every time—just enough to convince myself that the model hasn’t weirdly drifted. My evals feel vibe-y, still; but at least there are concrete tasks now. title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)
summary:
[1/2] Multi-agent coordination is a fun problem. We have this problem in the DocETL optimizer, where multiple agents are rewriting queries (in parallel) in our search for the most accurate & efficient query. Every task (ie hypothesizing and testing a rewrite) is very time consuming. When part of the task is coming up with the task, how do we make sure the agents don’t accidentally do the same task? At first we tried an optimistic concurrency control policy; have another agent just check whether a hypothesized rewrite has already been hypothesized before & abort if so. Unfortunately we realized that agents are “myopic” / they love to propose the same ideas (ie low diversity). So optimistic concurrency control led to lots of aborts & inefficiency. Then we tried a lock based approach (where the agent needs to acquire a lock before hypothesizing a rewrite, and releases after checking that the rewrite is unique). So rewrite hypothesis is serialized, and testing the rewrite (ie running the new query on samples to estimate accuracy and cost) is parallelized. Not bad, but not great. Can we do better? We realized that if we can make mutually exclusive classes of rewrites, we could have agents hypothesize a rewrite in each class in parallel. Two mutually exclusive classes of rewrites are: rewrites that _increase_ cost in hopes to increase accuracy (ie changing the LLM to a more $$ model); rewrites that _decrease_ cost in hope of maintaining the same accuracy (ie using embedding similarity to run the query on only top k documents instead of all docs). So now, two rewrite hypothesis generation steps can run in parallel (one agent for each class of rewrites), because we’ve designed them to “semantically” not conflict. And all the testing agents run in parallel, of course. It works well because testing is slower than hypothesis generation, but I know we are still underutilizing parallelization, and I am excited to keep working on this problem. Anyways, the interesting bit to me is: ultimately, by carefully designing what roles agents have, we are essentially partitioning the action space to achieve conflict free parallelism. It is reminiscent of CRDTs but for tasks/hypothetical actions instead of data.
Quoting @tldraw
There were many issues with this. What if two agents start working on the same task? Even if agents work on different tasks, how do they work together towards an overall goal? And in doing this, how do they coordinate between different parts of the overall goal?
────────
[2/2] You can learn more about our new optimizer in our new preprint:
(I will write a thread for this later once I’m back from vacation!)

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Yes and there is something new this time: we are allowing—and perhaps even embracing—ambiguity in program specification. For vibe coding, the best historical parallel I’ve found is predictive interaction from 10 years ago (Heer, Hellerstein, Kandel): to clean and transform their data, users point/highlight/demonstrate (ambiguously); the system suggests & refines the code based on the user’s interactions over time. Eg if the user wants to clean a bunch of URLs, they can highlight parts of URLs and get regex suggestions. The technical idea is to “lift” user interaction from writing code in a DSL to a simpler and natural visual domain. But rather than requiring the interactions in the visual domain & DSL be isomorphic (every interaction compiles to a statement), predictive interaction permits ambiguity, like AI-assisted coding, enabling more expressiveness and thereby improving productivity. But it also puts more burden on the user—because users need to learn how to provide interactions to get maximally-useful code suggestions. Users need to figure out the space of possible suggestions and disambiguate their prompt enough to land in the right subspace of AI-generated code. Just when users think they’ve figured it out, the LLMs change, and they have to re-figure it out. It’s hard! There’s lots of opportunity to design good lifted domains/DSLs/interfaces for vibe coding. I like some of the new primitives used by Claude code: eg planning, the 20-questions-like mini-conversations to better ground user prompts in the AI’s domain, ability to visualize conversation context and compact conversations at specific points, skills.
Quoting @random_walker
Today's conversations about AI-assisted programming are strikingly similar to those from decades ago about the choice between low-level languages like C versus high-level languages like Python. I was in college back then and some of our professors reassured us that the same issues had come up in the assembly-vs-compiled-languages debate from their own student days!
(If I were to guess, the switch from machine code to assembly even earlier must have led to similar discussions as well.)
The trade-off is always the same: productivity versus control. And the challenge is how to switch to the new paradigm in a way that enhances your skills (at least the ones you care about) instead of offloading too much and letting your skills atrophy.
Some approaches prove too hasty. Vibe coding is turning out to be a dead end because it offloads too much, just as WYSIWYG editors were a dead end for building web apps. But that doesn't mean we were forced to stick to raw HTML/JS: frameworks turned out to be the way forward.
When a new paradigm comes along, it takes months if not years of practice to figure out how to make it work for you. There are always many people dismissing the new thing too quickly. I was one! There are some embarrassing mailing list posts from the early 2000s in which I complained about Python and kids who can't code like real programmers do 🤦
While it's good to be open-minded, I'm not saying everyone needs to jump on the bandwagon. After all, low-level programming languages haven't gone away.
Of course, some people claim that AI is unlike previous waves of automation and can replace programmers. Maybe. The reason I disagree — and see AI as parallel to previous waves of productivity improvements in software engineering — is fourfold. (1) It's a matter of accountability, not just capability. (2) Writing the code was never the bottleneck. (3) I think we're underestimating the ability of experts to stay on top of even rapid AI capability increases by using these tools to dramatically expand what they can build, how well, and how quickly. (4) As these productivity improvements take shape, the potential growth in _demand_ for software is practically infinite, unlike trades where there is a fixed amount of work that needs to get done. For example, the idea that a car would contain ~100 million lines of code would have seemed head-explodingly implausible in the early days of programming.
Many people have observed that software seems to be one of the only fields that is undergoing a rapid transformation due to AI. The usual reason they give is that capability improvements in AI coding have been particularly rapid. I think this is only part of the story. The bigger factor is structural. Software has a history of repeatedly undergoing seismic shifts in the technologies of production, so it has never had time or the cultural inclination to ossify institutional processes around particular ways of doing things.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
This. It feels a bit unsettling in systems academia. Worse yet, the problems many papers try to optimize are already well-represented in the scientific literature, and even a good (albeit agent psychosis-induced) result often stems from the LLM having been trained on the solution.
I am absolutely in favor of pushing AI to solve hard problems, but I worry we are missing the plot. Maybe the current trend of writing papers using AI to (re)discover systems algorithms is on the path to AI truly discovering novel systems optimizations. If not, I hope we correct course soon.
Quoting @mitchellh
I've got an agent in a loop optimizing a renderer with the goal to minimize frame times (and tests to measure). It got times down from 88ms to 2ms and allocations down from ~150K to 500. Sounds good, right? Wrong. This is exactly why agent psychosis is a big fucking problem.
As an experiment, I rewrote the Ghostty core render state in Go, with access to identically laid out data structures as Ghostty and the exact same validation tests. I made a purposely naive renderer (simple, correct, but slow). 88ms per frame with 150,000 allocations (horrendous, lol)!
I then kickstarted a Ralph loop to bring the frame times down. I told it it can't modify input data structures or the public API or tests (they're correct), but it can do anything else it wants. It got to work.
It has worked for about 4 hours. I've spent around $350 on this experiment so far. The results?
88ms => 1.5ms
150K allocs => ~500 allocs
Incredible right? Nope.
My hand-written renderer I ported has frame times (same benchmark) of ~20us (0.020ms) and 0 allocations in the update path.
This is the problem with psychosis and lacking systems understanding. If you don't understand the system, you're going to accept that this is an incredible result. If you understand the system, you'll see better solutions immediately and can do roughly 75x better on throughput.
The people who blindly trust agent output are in the former camp. They're sheeple, overdrinking from a fountain of mediocrity.
Standard disclaimer: I use AI all the time. I like AI. The point I'm making is to not blindly accept results. Think. Analyze. Learn.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Some thoughts after building the Data Agent Benchmark
- build a "semantic layer" for all your data. a simple first pass can be done by running an LLM over a sample of data from each table, to come up with column annotations (commonly known as semantic types), possible functional dependencies (i.e., columns that depend on each other)
- use the semantic layer in the prompt for all questions
- enterprise data often needs to be cleaned. rather than try to clean all data up front (which is really difficult), keep a memory of subsets of data that need to be cleaned and how, so that the relevant data can be cleaned by the agent at query time
- extend the harness (i.e., codex, claude code) with a tool like DocETL or Claude workflows; basically the ability to run agentic map-reduce. often questions require reasoning about unstructured text columns to come up with the answer, which SQL or code doesn't support
Quoting @verrsane

I like this article. My perspective on how to effectively use AI coding agents in research is: remember the main goal of research, to improve our *human* understanding of the world. So I say, use agents as much as you want. But if you are not learning anything from your agents, slow down. Read outputs more carefully. Think of better ways to use the agents or steer them towards better directions. Invest in “skills” & practices that help you collaborate more efficiently with them. title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (2 tweets)

[1/2] I feel like this table is misleading. (I) It is not that novices write underspecified tasks; their methodology classifies underspecified prompts as “novice.”(ii) Every time a frontier lab says “expertise in the task,” they implicitly mean “expertise in the task AND the relevant data to analyze.” This assumption is trivially ok when there is no data to analyze, like in many coding tasks, but it’s unreasonable to assume people to be an expert in the specific dataset at hand. There are always ambiguities in real world data. Human data scientists take months to onboard. AI data scientists take $100k to build understanding of an enterprise-scale dataset (ie “semantic layer”), and still are no good.
The North Star for AI data analysts is to assist people who want to make data-driven decisions but don’t know what’s in their (real, messy) data. So perhaps it is a contrarian take for me to say that this “novice” prompt should actually work…and we have a long and exciting way to go to make this happen

2. a PE lesson‑plan generator for K‑12 teachers
3. a workers’ comp tool that drafts 50‑page medical reports
I believe this is a significant issue in AI Engineering and upstream of evals!

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Really nice essay (written by an undergraduate!) reflecting on how math is changing thanks to AI. I resonate a lot with the discussion on proof digestion & indigestion; I see analogs in my CS fields as well. One core idea of the essay is that AI put us in a world of abundant generations (proofs, code), and now we need to be able to digest these artifacts. Digestion is about teasing apart the “interesting” bits of the artifact (eg hard, novel, clever) and figuring out how to communicate these interesting bits to help other humans understand it. This is not easy. Takes people 10+ years to learn how to do this.
My thoughts: Digestion is human-centered — I never want to say “human in the loop” in the connotation of supervising / checking AI, because that’s just boring — and, in my opinion, requires a deep understanding of the pragmatics (in the linguistics definition) of the field. Pragmatics is about how we interpret language (not the semantics or literal meaning of language); all external context, social situations, etc. And AI just cannot develop this understanding of pragmatics yet; it lives in human-human interactions; related internet writing is mostly post-hoc reflections on pragmatics, not pragmatics itself.
So I resonate with this essay a lot; us next generation of scholars have an opportunity to think about and set new norms for digestion. I love that Apoorva separates verification from digestion; I think CS folks could benefit from this framing (too many people are focused on verifying AI generated code without thinking about how we are going to digest the millions of lines of code that meets some guarantee we may not even understand). But anyways, it can be an awesome next decade in research. And on a side note it’s great to see undergrads writing like this; the kids are alright 😆
Quoting @apoorvapanidapu
Earlier this month I volunteered at Stanford’s Future of Math symposium, and ever since, I've been puzzling through what it now means to pursue mathematics as a student in the age of AI. I wrote an essay to make sense of it all:

Quoting @AlexGDimakis
Best Paper Award to our ICML Workshop paper 'Fantastic Adaptive Taxonomies and How to Use Them'.
Let me summarize briefly what the paper is about: Failure taxonomies are becoming increasingly important.
We show that failure taxonomies can be used in multiple ways: 1. As a test-time scaling tool for best-of-N judges, 2) as a mutation feedback mechanism in optimization loops and 3) as runtime feedback for coding agents.
Previously people used MAST and other hand-made fixed failure taxonomies. In this paper we show how to create the failure taxonomy adaptively and dynamically: We observe agent rollouts and create an adaptive failure taxonomy, bespoke to the agent weaknesses and task challenges. These adaptive taxonomies give a massive boost: On Terminal Bench 2 we get 89.9% with Opus 4.6 / Forgecode harness and the adaptive taxonomy used with a Best-of-N Judge, outperforming fixed taxonomies by 15%. title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
hot take: sometimes I wonder if the uncanny valley is actually what we need, so we can more easily distinguish human-AI interaction from human-human interaction.
for example, writing. when I read something that feels mostly AI produced, I evaluate it differently.
instead of asking, “do I trust this person’s taste and understanding of the topic? so much that if I spend time reading this, will I learn something interesting?”
I switch to asking, “am I interested in this topic? and does the AI probably know more than I do here, without being so sloppy that I can still understand it?”
in short, the uncanny valley is a good cue to tell us how to evaluate or make sense of the information; the uncanny value cues the appropriate epistemic frame

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
In evals you have two totally different components: (1) discovery of what the failure modes are, (2) focused measurement of how prevalent these failure modes are—so you can prioritize what to fix. LLMs can help in (1) by finding some failure modes— but not all, since many failure modes are subjective/ about human interpretation of outputs. LLMs can help in (2) by looking at a trace and determining if the failure mode exists, rather than having a human look at every trace. But a big mistake people make is to have LLMs fully automate (1) and (2). LLM judge is a complement to human experts, not a replacement.
Quoting @isaac_flath
IMO people should think of LLM judge as instrumentation rather than as evals
The eval is human labels. LLM judge is instrumenting those human labels.
It's why skipping human labels to do LLM judge first makes no sense

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
we've been iterating a lot on how DocWriter internally represents a user's writing style!
the naive approach is to dump all a user's prior writing in context and pray the AI figures out how to sound like them. this doesn't really work. and the user can't just manually specify their style either, because nobody knows what their meaningful writing preferences (for an AI agent) actually are.
so we've built a multi-agent pipeline that runs lexical, grammatical, and discourse analyses on the user's writing, extracts specific patterns with evidence, and then surfaces them in a UI where the user can confirm or reject each pattern by comparing two passages side by side
TBD on how well it performs in our next round of user studies 😆 it feels like we are really trying to do anything possible to avoid fine-tuning, but perhaps we need to bite the bullet eventually

It is getting the data agents to obtain the (1) correct and (2) consistent answers --- which is very hard when data and context is so messy and fragmented. So the job of the data team is to "encode expert judgement into the infrastructure that allows agents to produce correct analysis *without* the data scientist in the room," as Ian says
all data products and UIs are going to undergo serious change. business decisions are made not by looking at a dashboard but by asking an agent what to do. on the pipelines/systems side: as Ian says, this means decision makers are not necessarily asking "SQL-shaped" questions. so the onus is on ETL to prepare the relevant data in a structured way, so agents can quickly query it on behalf of humans.
then, on the interface side: what is the UI going to do? a role of UI has always been to tap into the exceptional visual ability / pre-attentive processing of humans. dashboards were UI-for-exploration: they helped humans spot patterns in data themselves. but if the agent is the one looking at the data now, the UI has to serve a different purpose: helping humans grok and verify the agent's reasoning, not explore the data themselves. so maybe UI-for-verification is the new thing?
anyways we are in for a really exciting next few years

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Lots of disdain in the comments. It’s honestly a bit unnerving to read people’s negative reaction to a harmless plea to continue prioritizing sharing discoveries and results, as humanity has done for millennia. Maybe it’s easy to think that the authors are operating from a place of ego and jealousy, if they are Fields medalists, and therefore the general public doesn’t trust them. So let me try explaining as someone who has no career achievements, no stake in the frontier labs, and no jealousy because my peers are all early-career like me 😆
Academics are stewards of history. We have 3 jobs. (1) to train people / teach them what has been done in the past. (2) we make some discoveries ourselves, and (3) we regularly interact with our peers to learn about their discoveries; what tomorrow’s history may be. Many people think we just do (2), but in fact all 3 are important; otherwise we would be highly inefficient in problem-solving over the long term (centuries, millennia).
We cannot really make AI the stewards of history (there are capitalist and geopolitical incentives not to). If we rid the world of academic values, there may not be immediate consequences, but things will be very bad in the long term. Progress will stall. Eventually folks will realize we need a clear and continually-updating ledger of history (ie “memory” for the AI-pilled folks). It will take a lot of work to rebuild this culture from first principles
On the optimistic side I think academics have a golden opportunity to figure out how we can harness AI in pursuit of our values. We can probably keep more information in our history, disseminate info more broadly, review and validate each others’ discoveries faster, etc. But, given that academics are powerless compared to these trillion dollar companies, we can only do the best we can—speak up; discuss; educate the public about academic values (which we haven’t really had to do since ww2); and, honestly, pray
Quoting @AndrewCurran_
Twenty-five Fields Medal winners have published a joint declaration warning about what they see as a severe misalignment between AI companies and the mathematics community.

summary:
[1/2] Good take. A couple things to add. One, you can build a specialized inference engine while reusing components of vLLM or SGLang (e.g., the model loader and forward pass). Two, historically, applications have required fine-grained control over the buffer pool, and the KV cache is the inference analog. I suspect many applications and domains will need specialized KV cache management (e.g., data processing).
Quoting @JiaZhihao
I think this comes down to a classic systems tradeoff: generality vs. specialization. vLLM/SGLang cover a huge space of models × hardware × workloads. It’s hard for a single system to be best at every combination, and focusing on a narrower set gives you more room to optimize.
Historically, the challenge was engineering cost: optimizations for one configuration often need substantial rework for another. Coding agents are lowering that cost, which I suspect is one reason we’re seeing more specialized inference engines.
Fragmentation is worth discussing, but so is the value of specialization. Many of these engines can complement vLLM/SGLang, especially when users need more performance from a specific setup. My 2 cents.
────────
[2/2] Another thought: if you build a declarative DSL with inference in an operator, the “batch of independent string prompts” abstraction à la OpenAI API may not be the right intermediate layer to represent the domain specific program. The original sglang programming model seemed interesting here but not sure who is using it; if it’s actively supported

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Excited to share Quail, our new open source AI-SQL engine (a collab with Modal)! By planning queries and LLM inference together, it reaches 1B+ input tokens/min on one H100 for one query 😱🚀
AI-powered data operators create a new, interesting inference workload👇
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2103202562895904768/img/FbNZ_BqrVJdijHHa.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2103202562895904768/vid/avc1/446x270/FXf6vIfnmTN8dhw4.mp4?tag=29
────────
[2/8] We tried running all these LLM calls through hand-tuned vLLM baselines. On several queries, we observed lots of host overhead --- and, vLLM also discarded KV it needed later, causing it to process 50 million extra tokens. The query took 6.84 hours, when speed-of-light estimates suggested only 15 minutes...
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTAPkorbUAAhjpQ.jpg
────────
[3/8] AI-SQL lets users write queries like: "Find movie reviews that discuss the ending and recommend the movie", as, e.g., SELECT * FROM reviews where AI.IF("the review discusses the ending") AND AI.IF("the review recommends the movie").
Queries are insanely expensive! An AI filter calls an LLM for *every row*; an AI join can call it for every candidate pair (m * n rows). One query can generate millions of LLM calls, needing ultra-high throughput!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTAPWszbkAAbrQF.jpg
────────
[4/8] AI-SQL is such a special case workload, where you know nearly all requests up front (and can plan KV a lot better), and you care more about throughput, or executing the *entire* query as quickly as possible. And, requests are entirely prefill. Not like the interactive request setting that general-purpose inference engines are optimized for.
Turns out it makes sense to build a specialized inference engine here, motivating Quail.
────────
[5/8] On 29 benchmark queries, Quail is 1.84x faster than hand-tuned vLLM baselines. On our largest medical reports query, it’s 14x faster (only 29 mins compared to 6.84 hours)! We also have considerably less KV regret.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTAUDAdaAAAnyt8.jpg
────────
[6/8] Quail combines good query planning with good inference: e.g., it orders AI operators, pipelines rows so their KV stays in GPU HBM, and batches work to keep the GPU busy. For AI joins, we even use some fun tree attention tricks (c.f. SpecInfer, Hydragen) to reuse forward pass work when comparing one document with many others!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTAT9MCboAEfy6D.jpg
────────
[7/8] We still have lots more to develop; for example, a use case where vLLM wins is on analyzing agent traces (that have matching prefixes across different rows). Its automatic prefix cache catches those matches; Quail doesn’t yet. vLLM is 2.32x faster on one such query. So automatic prefix caching is definitely on our roadmap.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTAUlB0bMAAOhPK.jpg
────────
[8/8] Today, Quail supports AI filters and joins -- and we are adding much more. The code is MIT licensed. We'd love to hear what you try with it! This is a really fun collaboration with inference 🐐 @charles_irl from Modal; look out for their post :-)

amazing stuff! really deep integration between inference engine and query engine.
they use vllm internals as a library, but replace the general purpose serving scheduler with one designed for batched, high throughput, prefill only queries used for ai filters/joins. their custom scheduler allows for workload aware kv cache management and their custom execution layer has attention kernel implementations that avoid repeatedly reading the same shared kvs across multiple queries.
reminds me a bit of workload aware inference schedulers for agent workloads ( that have session aware kv ttls to avoid evicting cache during environment interactions. will likely see more custom inference schedulers as we get more creative with how llms are used.
great timing for this project, especially with the launch of jev, showing the utility of classification in llm workflows. there are so many obvious applications of infra like this for production agent observability, which can be used for harness improvement and data curation for post training.
fenic took a lot of inspiration from docetl and lotus. we were primarily focused on exploring the ai dataframe/query interface and barely scratched the surface with logical plan optimizations. excited to see where ai in data processing libraries/dbs go as the physical execution layer become more specialized too.
wonder the extent to which there is room for datafusion integration to enable joint optimization across the inference engine and query engine.

When reviewing production traces, it's costly to check every trace, so you want to find the ones most likely to reveal failures. The usual approach is to explore broadly at first, then focus on signals that indicate problems.

Shreya Shankar suggests starting with broad exploration, then using signals to pick traces likely to show failures. Importantly, you keep some random traces in every batch to catch new, unexpected issues. This balances targeted review with discovery, making the process more efficient.

title: Shreya Shankar (@sh_reya)
summary:
Finally a use case that makes sense for the jev api in the database — Postgres (an OLTP database) is the right form factor. Follow along with our Quail project for how we are designing for the OLAP case 🌟
Quoting @_avichawla
Another insane Jev use case!
Traditional database filters need precise, predefined conditions. But many questions are semantic:
- Is this article mainly about software engineering?
- Which topic best describes it?
- How technically deep does it appear?
These usually require moving rows into application code, invoking a model, parsing its output, and writing the result back.
pg-jev is an open-source Postgres extension that exposes Jev through SQL functions.
- jev() works inside WHERE
- jev_prob() returns a probability
- jev_choice() selects a label
- jev_score() ranks rows across ordered levels.
It needs no vector column or embedding index.
Under the hood, pg-jev batches rows, sends them to Jev, and returns typed answers that SQL can filter, sort, group, and combine with exact predicates.
The recording below runs it against real Hacker News stories stored in Postgres.
It first shows the rows, then asks Jev to find software-engineering stories, classify them by topic, and rank them by technical depth. The final query reports requests, tokens, cost, and cache hits from the database session.
GitHub repo:
(don't forget to star it ⭐)
Postgres keeps the data and controls the query, while Jev handles the part SQL cannot express as a deterministic condition.
If you want to understand what Jev is doing under the hood, I also wrote a hands-on guide to building a Jev-style model with open models, entirely locally.
Read it below.

Found this video interesting (especially as someone who hasn't been a user of BI tools for 5+ years). Some interesting implications from this Rippling case study (all of these are my opinions):
- For agents, choosing a tool / MCP and choosing what data to retrieve start to look like the same problem: both are pieces of context needed to answer a question. The old boundary between "business logic" and “data” gets blurrier.
- Also interesting: Rippling’s data team still manually inspects agent queries and creates new rollup tables when patterns emerge. Where are the materialized view database fiends -- they would find this very fascinating!!
- I could be wrong but: it feels like trad ELT is mostly push based: i.e., humans anticipate questions and build tables / dashboards. Agents make BI much more pull based than in the past: the question arrives first, then the system figures out what data, transformations, and tools it needs.
- And perhaps one reason why existing semantic layer tools aren't great yet: not all past queries are equally useful signals. Perhaps we cares more about which queries led to useful business actions, not just query history in aggregate.

summary:
[1/4] We now support prefix sharing in Quail, our open-source AI-SQL engine! In this example tagging 1,772 long agent traces with issue types using qwen3-4b: we compute 3x fewer tokens and the query runs 2.6x faster ⏩👇
🎬 https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2107873366376075264/img/pN5wITyJzYrtgPY_.jpg | https://video-s.twimg.com/amplify_video/2107873366376075264/vid/avc1/480x270/H3Sq1kfIMf3Qkl0W.mp4?tag=29
────────
[2/4] Try it today at and star to follow along!!
────────
[3/4] Prefix sharing is expressed simply, as a rule in Quail's query optimizer. That is, Quail will automatically determine whether to enable prefix sharing, depending on how much overlap there is between documents and whether the benefit outweighs the cost of the KV writes:
────────
[4/4] Quail's prefix sharing is basically the same as prefix & radix caching techniques, adopted by all inference engines. But since we receive LLM calls through AI-SQL queries, we can plan all the sharing upfront during query optimization. Reuse doesn't depend on LLM request arrival order or KV cache eviction.
Learn more:
clean_summary:
When you run many similar AI queries, like tagging 1,772 agent traces, you usually repeat a lot of token computations, which wastes time and resources. Shreya Shankar shows that prefix sharing can reduce this by computing 3 times fewer tokens and making the query 2.6 times faster.

Quail, an open-source AI-SQL engine, implements prefix sharing as a rule in its query optimizer. It decides automatically when to share prefixes based on document overlap and cost. Unlike usual caching that depends on request order or cache eviction, Quail plans all sharing upfront during optimization, making reuse more efficient and predictable.
